stem: A data engineering team needs to ingest high-throughput clickstream data and also wants to reuse existing Apache Kafka consumer applications with minimal code changes. Which AWS service should they select as the streaming ingestion layer to minimize application rewrite effort while still receiving a fully managed broker service?

choices.text: Amazon SQS
AWS DMS
Amazon MSK
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Amazon MSK ingests high-throughput streams and lets the team reuse existing Kafka tools, clients, and connectors.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SQS: queue, not Kafka.
• DMS: database migration.
• Kinesis: different API, can't reuse Kafka tooling.

Key takeaway: reuse Kafka ecosystem → MSK.

stem: Every insert, update, or delete in a DynamoDB orders table must trigger processing within seconds, in order per order ID, with before and after images available to the consumer. Which design fits?

choices.text: A Lambda function scanning the table every minute for changes
A CloudWatch alarm on the table's consumed write capacity
An S3 export of the table every hour processed by Glue
DynamoDB Streams (NEW_AND_OLD_IMAGES) with a Lambda mapping

explanation:
Why this is correct:
DynamoDB Streams captures item-level changes in order per partition key, and the NEW_AND_OLD_IMAGES view type provides both images. A Lambda event source mapping processes records within seconds.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Scanning: expensive and misses intermediate changes.
• Hourly export: not near real time.
• Capacity alarm: signals volume, not individual changes.

Key takeaway: item-level change events → Streams + Lambda.

stem: After a full load of an on-premises Oracle database to S3, ongoing changes must keep flowing to S3 with minutes of latency until cutover, with no custom code. Which approach fits?

choices.text: A Glue job that reruns a full extract every hour
Nightly Oracle Data Pump exports copied to S3
A Snowball Edge device shipped weekly with new data
A DMS full load plus CDC task to an S3 target

explanation:
Why this is correct:
DMS can perform a full load and then capture ongoing changes (CDC) from Oracle logs, writing them continuously to S3 targets.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Nightly exports: day-level latency.
• Hourly full extracts: heavy load and still delayed.
• Snowball: offline, not continuous.

Key takeaway: ongoing replication → DMS CDC.

stem: Marketing needs Salesforce opportunities copied to S3 hourly, only changed records, with field mapping and filtering, and without writing code or running servers. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS DataSync with a Salesforce location
Amazon AppFlow with incremental transfer
An EC2 cron script using the Salesforce SDK
A Glue job calling the Salesforce REST API

explanation:
Why this is correct:
AppFlow is a managed integration service for SaaS applications such as Salesforce, supporting scheduled incremental transfers, field mapping, and filters to destinations such as S3.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Glue with the REST API: custom code.
• EC2 cron: servers and code.
• DataSync: file and object storage, not SaaS APIs.

Key takeaway: SaaS → AWS without code → AppFlow.

stem: A Glue job must start within seconds when a file lands under s3://raw/orders/, but only for .csv files, and must not start twice for the same object. Which design fits?

choices.text: A CloudWatch alarm on the bucket's object count
A Glue trigger that runs the job every five minutes
S3 events to EventBridge, filtered to start the job
A crawler scheduled every minute that starts the job

explanation:
Why this is correct:
S3 can send events to EventBridge, where rules filter on prefix and suffix and start a Glue job or workflow. Idempotency (for example, job bookmarks or tracking processed keys) prevents double processing.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Five-minute schedule: not within seconds.
• Crawler every minute: catalogs schemas, not a trigger mechanism.
• Object count alarm: coarse and delayed.

Key takeaway: event-driven ETL starts → S3 events via EventBridge.

stem: A data engineer currently uses a Lambda function with an internal sleep loop to poll an API every 15 minutes for new data. Leadership asks for a more cost-efficient, AWS-native way to invoke the ingestion function on a fixed 15-minute interval. Which change best meets this goal?

choices.text: Increase the Lambda timeout to 15 minutes and keep the sleep loop
Replace the loop with an EventBridge Scheduler rule
Move the polling logic into an RDS stored procedure
Use S3 Transfer Acceleration

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An EventBridge schedule invokes the function periodically, replacing a costly sleep loop that pays for idle time.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Longer timeout with sleep: still wasteful.
• RDS stored procedure: wrong tool.
• Transfer Acceleration: unrelated.

Key takeaway: periodic polling → schedules, not sleep loops.

stem: A team already has 40 Airflow DAGs using Python operators and wants to move them to AWS without rewriting, with managed scaling and patching. Which service fits?

choices.text: Airflow self-managed on EC2 instances
AWS Step Functions with each DAG rewritten as ASL
Amazon Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow
AWS Glue workflows replacing the Airflow DAGs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
MWAA runs Apache Airflow as a managed service, so existing DAGs and operators can move with minimal change while AWS handles infrastructure.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Step Functions rewrite: requires rewriting every DAG.
• Glue workflows: limited to Glue jobs and crawlers.
• Self-managed: patching and scaling remain your job.

Key takeaway: existing Airflow → MWAA.

stem: A Lambda function consuming from a Kinesis Data Stream is falling behind, and CloudWatch shows the IteratorAge metric steadily increasing, even though the function's own duration is short and its logic is already efficient. What is the most likely configuration change to reduce processing lag?

choices.text: Reduce the number of shards in the stream
Decrease the Lambda function's memory allocation
Switch consumers to standard throughput only
Raise batch size and parallelization factor

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A larger batch size and the parallelization factor (multiple concurrent batches per shard) increase Lambda throughput from Kinesis.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Fewer shards: less throughput.
• Less memory: slower.
• Standard throughput only: doesn't add parallelism.

Key takeaway: Lambda lag on Kinesis → batch size + parallelization factor.

stem: Producers writing to an Amazon Kinesis Data Stream in provisioned mode intermittently receive ProvisionedThroughputExceededException errors during traffic spikes. Which combination of actions addresses this without redesigning the application? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Increase the number of shards, or switch the stream to On-Demand capacity mode
Decrease the data retention period to 24 hours
Implement exponential backoff and retry in the producer
Disable server-side encryption on the stream
Omit the partition key from records

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Throughput exceptions mean producers exceed shard limits. Add shards or use on-demand mode, and implement exponential backoff and retries in producers.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Shorter retention: unrelated.
• Disable encryption: unrelated.
• Omit partition key: required.

Key takeaway: write throttling → capacity + backoff.

stem: Several consumer applications need to read the same Amazon Kinesis Data Stream simultaneously at full throughput (2 MB/sec per shard each) without contending for the shared 2 MB/sec-per-shard read throughput. Which feature should be enabled?

choices.text: On-Demand capacity mode
Server-side encryption with KMS
Enhanced fan-out
Kinesis Data Firehose delivery

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Enhanced fan-out gives each registered consumer its own 2 MB/s per-shard read throughput, so many consumers don't compete.

Why the other options are wrong:
• On-demand: write capacity.
• KMS encryption: security.
• Firehose: delivery.

Key takeaway: many consumers → enhanced fan-out.

stem: Hundreds of IoT gateways write readings to one Kinesis stream, and multiple consumers (analytics, alerting, archive) read the same data independently at full speed. Which patterns describe this?

choices.text: Batch uploads to S3 processed by a nightly job
Point-to-point queues from each gateway to each consumer
Fan-in to the stream; fan-out to consumers
Fan-out from gateways; fan-in to consumers via polling

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Many producers writing to one stream is fan-in. Several independent consumers each reading the full stream is fan-out, and enhanced fan-out gives each consumer dedicated throughput.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Reversed terms: incorrect.
• Point-to-point: an explosion of connections.
• Nightly batch: not streaming.

Key takeaway: many-to-one = fan-in; one-to-many = fan-out.

stem: A team wants the ability to reprocess up to 30 days of historical events from a Kinesis Data Stream if a downstream bug is discovered, without re-ingesting from the original source systems. What is the primary tradeoff of extending the stream's retention period to 30 days to support this replay capability?

choices.text: Extended retention automatically deletes data after 7 days regardless of the setting
Retention has no cost impact but requires re-sharding
Retention period changes require re-creating the stream
Extended retention beyond 24 hours incurs additional per-shard-hour storage charges

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Retention beyond 24 hours (up to 365 days) costs extra per shard-hour, and longer-term retention adds per-GB charges.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Deletes after 7 days: configurable.
• No cost: extra cost applies.
• Requires recreating the stream: no.

Key takeaway: replay window costs money.

stem: A stream job computes a 5-minute rolling average per device and must survive restarts without losing the window. What kind of processing is this, and what supports it?

choices.text: Batch processing in a nightly Glue job
Stateless filtering at the Firehose stage with a Lambda transform
Stateless processing with a Lambda per record
Stateful processing with checkpointed state (Flink)

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Windowed aggregations keep state across records. Managed Service for Apache Flink manages keyed state and checkpoints/snapshots so windows survive restarts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Stateless Lambda: no built-in window state.
• Nightly batch: not rolling in real time.
• Firehose filtering: stateless transformation.

Key takeaway: windows and aggregations → stateful streaming.
services: Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink

stem: An AWS DMS replication instance in a VPC must connect to an on-premises SQL Server database over a Site-to-Site VPN, and the on-premises firewall administrator requires that only a specific, stable IP address be allowlisted. Which configuration ensures the replication instance's traffic presents a consistent, allowlistable address?

choices.text: Rotate the replication instance's IP address daily
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the replication instance
Give the instance a fixed private IP the firewall allows
Disable the VPC security group entirely

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Assigning the replication instance a fixed private IP (or using its static private address) lets the on-premises firewall allow it reliably over DX or VPN.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Rotate IP daily: breaks rules.
• Transfer Acceleration: S3 only.
• Disable security groups: unsafe.

Key takeaway: stable IPs for firewall rules.

stem: A retail company wants to query live clickstream events arriving on an Amazon Kinesis Data Stream directly from Amazon Redshift using SQL, with sub-minute latency, without first landing the data in Amazon S3 or running a separate ETL job. Which Redshift capability supports this?

choices.text: Redshift federated query to RDS
Amazon Redshift Serverless snapshot restore
Redshift streaming ingestion into a materialized view
Redshift Spectrum

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Redshift streaming ingestion reads Kinesis directly into a materialized view with low latency, without staging in S3.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Federated query to RDS: not streams.
• Snapshot restore: backups.
• Spectrum: S3 data.

Key takeaway: stream into Redshift → streaming ingestion.

stem: New CSV folders arrive daily with occasional new columns. The team needs tables discoverable in Athena and a nightly job converting them to Parquet. Which Glue components do what?

choices.text: A crawler does both cataloging and Parquet conversion
An ETL job catalogs schemas; a crawler converts to Parquet
DataBrew catalogs; the crawler converts the files
Crawler catalogs schemas; an ETL job converts to Parquet

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Crawlers infer schemas and update the Data Catalog, and ETL jobs read, transform, and write data such as converting CSV to Parquet.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Swapped roles: crawlers don't transform data.
• Crawler doing both: crawlers don't write data files.
• DataBrew cataloging: DataBrew prepares data; crawlers catalog.

Key takeaway: crawlers describe data; jobs change data.

stem: A nightly Spark job processes 40 TB of logs using custom JARs and Spark tuning. The team wants the lowest cost and no cluster running between runs. Which option fits?

choices.text: A permanently running EMR cluster sized for peak
Amazon Redshift, loading 40 TB before each query
Lambda functions processing each log file in parallel on a schedule
A transient EMR cluster (or EMR Serverless) with Spot

explanation:
Why this is correct:
EMR supports custom Spark configuration and JARs. Transient clusters or EMR Serverless avoid idle cost, and Spot capacity lowers compute cost.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Permanent cluster: pays for idle time.
• Redshift: a warehouse, not a Spark engine.
• Lambda: limits make 40 TB Spark-style processing impractical.

Key takeaway: big Spark batch without idle cost → transient EMR or EMR Serverless.

stem: A Lambda-based ingestion function calls a third-party REST API that enforces a strict rate limit and returns HTTP 429 responses when exceeded. The function currently retries immediately in a tight loop upon failure, causing repeated 429 errors. What is the best fix?

choices.text: Increase the Lambda function's reserved concurrency to call the API faster
Use exponential backoff with jitter and Retry-After
Switch the ingestion trigger from EventBridge to S3 Event Notifications
Disable retries entirely so the loop stops

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Exponential backoff with jitter, honoring the API's Retry-After or rate limits, avoids overwhelming a rate-limited API.

Why the other options are wrong:
• More concurrency: more rate limit errors.
• Change trigger: unrelated.
• Disable retries: loses data.

Key takeaway: rate-limited APIs → backoff with jitter.

stem: An AWS Glue batch job runs nightly against an S3 data lake and should process only files that have arrived since the previous run, avoiding reprocessing of already-ingested files. Which Glue configuration option enables this incremental behavior?

choices.text: Job bookmarks
DynamicFrame partitioning
Glue Data Catalog versioning
G.2X worker type

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Glue job bookmarks track processed data so each run handles only new files.

Why the other options are wrong:
• DynamicFrame partitioning: layout.
• Catalog versioning: schema history.
• Worker type: capacity.

Key takeaway: incremental processing → job bookmarks.

stem: A data engineering team runs containerized Apache Spark transformation jobs and wants Kubernetes-native orchestration with the ability to use existing Kubernetes operators and custom resource definitions for Spark job management. Which AWS compute option best fits this requirement over a simpler container orchestrator?

choices.text: Amazon EKS
Amazon EMR Serverless
AWS Lambda container images
Amazon ECS with Fargate

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Amazon EKS runs containerized Spark with Kubernetes-native scheduling and tooling (EMR on EKS is another option).

Why the other options are wrong:
• EMR Serverless: no Kubernetes.
• Lambda: not for Spark.
• ECS Fargate: not Kubernetes.

Key takeaway: Kubernetes-native Spark → EKS.

stem: A Glue job must read from SQL Server on premises over Direct Connect, with no internet exposure. Which configuration fits?

choices.text: A crawler run from the internet-facing Glue endpoint
A Glue job without a connection, using the public DNS name
A Glue JDBC connection in your VPC subnet
A public endpoint for SQL Server allowed from Glue's IPs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A Glue connection specifies a VPC, subnet, and security group, so the job's ENIs run in your VPC and reach on-premises databases over Direct Connect or VPN routes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Public endpoint: violates no internet exposure.
• Crawler from the internet: same problem.
• No connection: the job can't reach private networks.

Key takeaway: private data sources → Glue connection in your VPC.

stem: An analyst's desktop BI tool must query Redshift Serverless securely with the analyst's corporate identity, without a shared database password. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Redshift ODBC/JDBC driver with IdP federation
Share the admin user's password with each analyst
Export the tables to CSV and email them to analysts
Query through the Data API with the root user

explanation:
Why this is correct:
BI tools connect to Redshift through its ODBC or JDBC drivers, which support IAM or identity provider federation, so each analyst uses their own identity with temporary credentials.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Shared admin password: no accountability.
• CSV exports: stale and insecure.
• Root user: never for routine access.

Key takeaway: desktop BI → driver + federated identity.

stem: A single AWS Glue Spark ETL job must join order data from Amazon Redshift with customer profile data stored as Parquet files in Amazon S3 in one transformation step. Which Glue capability enables reading from both sources within the same job?

choices.text: Multiple connections and DynamicFrames in one job
Using S3 Batch Operations to copy Redshift data into S3 first
Running two separate Lambda functions and merging results client-side
Enabling Redshift Spectrum exclusively, bypassing Glue entirely

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A Glue job can define multiple connections and create DynamicFrames from Redshift and other sources, then join them in one job.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 Batch Operations: object actions.
• Two Lambdas: limited and complex.
• Spectrum only: doesn't join external sources this way.

Key takeaway: multi-source ETL in one Glue job.

stem: A nightly batch transformation job is not time-critical and can tolerate variable start times. The team wants to reduce the cost of running this AWS Glue job by roughly 30-40% compared to standard execution. Which Glue execution option should they enable?

choices.text: G.2X worker type exclusively
Flexible execution (Glue Flex)
Job bookmarks
Increasing the number of DPUs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Glue Flex execution runs non-urgent jobs on spare capacity at lower cost, with variable start times.

Why the other options are wrong:
• G.2X: capacity.
• Bookmarks: incremental.
• More DPUs: more cost.

Key takeaway: non-urgent Glue jobs → Flex.

stem: A few-KB JSON file lands a few times per hour and must be normalized within seconds, with near-zero cost when idle. Which option fits?

choices.text: A Lambda function triggered by the S3 event
An EC2 instance polling the bucket every few seconds
An EMR cluster running continuously
A Glue Spark job started for each file

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Lambda starts in milliseconds, scales to zero, and handles small transformations cheaply when triggered by S3 events.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Glue Spark per file: startup overhead and minimum billing for tiny files.
• EMR continuous: idle cost.
• EC2 polling: idle cost and delay.

Key takeaway: tiny, sporadic transforms → Lambda.

stem: Athena queries on a CSV data lake scan full files though they select 5 of 80 columns, and most filter by date. Which change cuts cost MOST?

choices.text: Convert to partitioned, compressed Parquet
Convert the files to JSON Lines
Increase the Athena workgroup's data scan limit
Gzip the CSV files in place

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Parquet is columnar and compressed, so Athena reads only the needed columns. Partitioning by date prunes files. Together these can reduce scanned data dramatically.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Gzip CSV: smaller files but still full-row scans.
• JSON: row-based and larger.
• Scan limit: caps usage, doesn't reduce it.

Key takeaway: Athena cost = bytes scanned → columnar + partitions.

stem: Internal apps need a secured REST endpoint returning curated customer aggregates stored in S3, with per-app throttling and IAM auth. Which design fits?

choices.text: An EC2 web server with a shared password
Direct Athena access granted to each internal application
API Gateway with a Lambda backend querying the data
Public S3 URLs for each aggregate file

explanation:
Why this is correct:
API Gateway provides the REST interface with IAM authorization and throttling, and Lambda queries or reads the curated data (for example, via Athena or pre-built files).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Public S3 URLs: no auth or throttling.
• Direct Athena: not a REST API, and grants broader access.
• EC2 with a shared password: operational overhead and weak security.

Key takeaway: data as a secured API → API Gateway + Lambda.

stem: A new workload ingests structured relational data, semi-structured JSON logs, and unstructured images, arriving at highly variable rates that spike unpredictably during marketing campaigns. Which characterization of this workload should most influence the architecture decision toward flexible, scalable, schema-on-read storage and processing?

choices.text: Low variety with predictable batch arrival
A single data type with a fixed schema
High variety and high velocity variability
Low volume and constant velocity only

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Mixed structured, semi-structured, and unstructured data arriving at varying rates means high variety and variable velocity.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Low variety: incorrect.
• Single type: incorrect.
• Low volume constant velocity: incorrect.

Key takeaway: characterize data by volume, velocity, and variety.

stem: A data engineering pipeline needs to extract structured entities, such as product names and sentiment, from unstructured customer review text stored in S3 as part of a transformation step, using a foundation model without managing the model's infrastructure. Which AWS service should be integrated into the transformation step?

choices.text: Amazon Bedrock
Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics
AWS Glue Schema Registry
Amazon Redshift Spectrum

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Bedrock foundation models can extract structured entities from unstructured text within a pipeline.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Kinesis Analytics: stream SQL.
• Schema Registry: schemas.
• Spectrum: S3 queries.

Key takeaway: entity extraction from text → FMs via Bedrock (or Comprehend).

stem: A Glue Spark script needs to gracefully handle records with inconsistent or evolving schemas while reading from a semi-structured JSON source, before optionally converting to a strict schema later in the script. Which Glue-native abstraction is best suited for this initial read?

choices.text: A NumPy array
A standard Spark DataFrame only
DynamicFrame
A Pandas DataFrame

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Glue DynamicFrames handle inconsistent or evolving schemas with choice types, without failing.

Why the other options are wrong:
• NumPy arrays: no.
• Standard DataFrame: needs fixed schema.
• Pandas: not distributed.

Key takeaway: messy schemas in Glue → DynamicFrame.

stem: Analysts frequently filter a large S3-based sales dataset in Athena by both year/month and country. Which S3 partitioning strategy would most improve query performance and reduce cost for these access patterns?

choices.text: Partition by file size only
Partition the data by year, month, and country in the S3 key structure
Partition only by a randomly generated UUID
Store all data in a single unpartitioned prefix

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Partitioning by year, month, and country in the S3 path lets Athena prune partitions for common filters.

Why the other options are wrong:
• File size: not a filter.
• UUID: useless for pruning.
• Unpartitioned: full scans.

Key takeaway: partition by common filter columns.

stem: A team runs sporadic Spark transformation jobs with unpredictable schedules and does not want to manage cluster sizing or scaling, but occasionally needs fine-grained control over specific EC2 instance types and custom AMIs for specialized hardware. Which statement correctly describes the tradeoff between EMR Serverless and EMR on EC2 here?

choices.text: Both options provide identical levels of infrastructure control
EMR Serverless requires manual cluster provisioning while EMR on EC2 is fully automatic
EMR on EC2 cannot run Spark jobs, only Hive
EMR Serverless removes cluster management but offers less control

explanation:
Why this is correct:
EMR Serverless removes cluster management and scales automatically for sporadic jobs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Identical control: EC2 gives more control.
• Serverless needs provisioning: reversed.
• EC2 can't run Spark: false.

Key takeaway: sporadic Spark → EMR Serverless.

stem: An AWS Glue job configured with a JDBC connection to an Amazon RDS MySQL database fails with a connection timeout error, even though the RDS instance is running and credentials are correct. What is the most likely root cause?

choices.text: The JDBC driver version is newer than the MySQL engine version
The RDS instance has Multi-AZ enabled
The job's subnet lacks a route or SG rule to RDS
The Glue Data Catalog database name does not match the JDBC connection name

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A JDBC connection timeout from Glue usually means the job's subnet lacks a route or security group rule to reach RDS.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Driver newer: different error.
• Multi-AZ: unrelated.
• Catalog name mismatch: different error.

Key takeaway: Glue connection timeouts → networking.

stem: Analysts run a handful of ad hoc queries each month against 5 TB of historical Parquet in S3. They want no infrastructure and cost only when querying. Which option fits?

choices.text: Athena, paying per data scanned
Loading the data into RDS for PostgreSQL
A permanent EMR cluster with Presto
A provisioned Redshift cluster running all month

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Athena is serverless and charges by data scanned, which fits infrequent queries on data already in S3.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Provisioned Redshift: pays around the clock.
• Permanent EMR: idle cost.
• RDS load: unsuitable for 5 TB analytics.

Key takeaway: occasional queries on S3 → Athena.

stem: A Glue Spark job reading millions of very small files, a few KB each, from S3 runs much slower than expected, spending excessive time on file listing and task scheduling overhead relative to actual data volume. Which technique would most directly address this performance issue?

choices.text: Compact small files, or use groupFiles when reading
Convert the files to JSON format
Disable job bookmarks
Increase the job's DPU count without changing file structure

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Many tiny files add per-file overhead. Compact them into larger files, or use Glue's file grouping options.

Why the other options are wrong:
• JSON: no help.
• Disable bookmarks: no help.
• More DPUs: treats symptom.

Key takeaway: small files → compaction/grouping.

stem: An application needs to run SQL queries against Amazon Redshift asynchronously over HTTPS from an AWS Lambda function, without managing persistent JDBC or ODBC database connections or connection pooling. Which feature should be used?

choices.text: Redshift Spectrum
A JDBC connection pool inside the Lambda function
Amazon RDS Proxy
The Amazon Redshift Data API

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The Redshift Data API runs SQL asynchronously over HTTPS without managing connections or drivers.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Spectrum: S3 queries.
• JDBC pool in Lambda: connection management.
• RDS Proxy: not for Redshift.

Key takeaway: HTTP SQL to Redshift → Data API.

stem: A pipeline combines RDS order rows, JSON clickstream events, and product images. Which data characteristic drives the need for different storage and processing tools?

choices.text: Velocity of the order database's writes
Veracity of the clickstream's source systems
Variety of data structures
Volume of the RDS database alone

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Variety describes different data structures (tables, JSON, images), each needing suitable formats, stores, and processing.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Velocity: speed of arrival.
• Veracity: trustworthiness.
• Volume: size.

Key takeaway: different shapes of data = variety.

stem: A pipeline calls five AWS APIs in sequence, retries failed steps with backoff, branches on results, and waits for a Glue job to finish, all without servers. Which service fits?

choices.text: A cron job on EC2 calling the AWS CLI
A single Lambda function that sleeps between API calls
AWS Step Functions with service integrations
MWAA running on the largest environment size

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Step Functions orchestrates AWS APIs with built-in retries, branching, and .sync integrations that wait for jobs such as Glue to complete.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Sleeping Lambda: 15-minute limit and paid waiting.
• MWAA: possible but heavier for a handful of steps.
• EC2 cron: servers and custom retry logic.

Key takeaway: serverless orchestration of AWS calls → Step Functions.

stem: A pipeline must start a Step Functions state machine whenever a specific custom application event is published, and also route that event to multiple independent targets for auditing and parallel processing. Which service enables this pattern?

choices.text: Amazon EventBridge
Amazon SNS used exclusively
AWS Systems Manager Automation
AWS Config rules

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An EventBridge rule matching the custom event can start the Step Functions state machine.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SNS only: no direct pattern routing to Step Functions in this way.
• SSM Automation: not an event router.
• Config: compliance.

Key takeaway: event-driven orchestration → EventBridge.

stem: A team is orchestrating a pipeline entirely with a single Lambda function that sequentially calls other Lambda functions and waits for each to complete, with the whole workflow sometimes running over 20 minutes. What is the primary limitation of this approach compared to using Step Functions?

choices.text: Its 15-minute timeout can break long workflows
Step Functions cannot invoke Lambda functions
Lambda has no way to pass data between invocations
Lambda functions cannot invoke other Lambda functions at all

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A single orchestrating Lambda is bounded by the 15-minute maximum execution time, so long pipelines fail. Step Functions avoids this.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Step Functions can't invoke Lambda: it can.
• No data passing: possible but not the main limit.
• Lambda can't invoke Lambda: it can.

Key takeaway: orchestration beyond 15 minutes → Step Functions.

stem: A high-volume streaming enrichment workflow needs to execute millions of short-duration workflow executions per day at the lowest possible cost, and does not require exactly-once execution semantics or 90-day execution history retention. Which Step Functions workflow type should be used?

choices.text: Express Workflows
Activity tasks with EC2 workers
Standard Workflows
A state machine with a zero-second wait state

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Express Workflows are designed for high-volume, short-duration executions at low cost.

Why the other options are wrong:
• EC2 activity workers: heavy.
• Standard: costly at this volume.
• Zero-second wait: meaningless.

Key takeaway: millions of short workflows → Express.

stem: A Step Functions state machine invokes a Lambda function that occasionally fails due to a transient downstream service error. The team wants automatic retries a limited number of times with increasing wait intervals, then a fallback error-handling branch. Which Step Functions constructs should be used together?

choices.text: A Parallel state with no error handling
A Retry field with backoff rate on the state, combined with a Catch field routing to a fallback state
Increasing only the Lambda function's memory
A Map state iterating over an empty array

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A Retry field with interval, backoff rate, and max attempts handles transient errors, and a Catch routes persistent failures.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Parallel without handling: no.
• More memory: doesn't fix transient failures.
• Empty Map: no.

Key takeaway: transient failures → Retry + Catch.

stem: When a pipeline fails, on-call engineers need an email and a remediation Lambda must run, both from one published message, each independently. Which service fits?

choices.text: An SNS topic with email and Lambda subscriptions
An SQS queue read by both the engineers and Lambda
A Kinesis stream consumed by an email client
A CloudWatch dashboard linked from the runbook

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SNS fans out one message to multiple subscribers, such as email and Lambda, each receiving a copy.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SQS: each message is consumed once, not by both.
• Kinesis: not an email notification tool.
• Dashboard: passive.

Key takeaway: one event, many recipients → SNS.

stem: A producer generates tasks faster than a Lambda transformer can handle, and tasks are lost when Lambda throttles. Tasks must never be lost and should be processed as capacity allows. Which change fits?

choices.text: Increase the Lambda timeout to 15 minutes
Call Lambda synchronously in a tight retry loop
Add more memory to the Lambda function
SQS between producer and Lambda, with a DLQ

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SQS buffers tasks durably, Lambda polls at a controlled concurrency, and a DLQ captures messages that repeatedly fail.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Longer timeout: doesn't solve throttling.
• Tight retries: add pressure.
• More memory: doesn't add concurrency capacity.

Key takeaway: decouple producers from consumers with a queue.

stem: Within an AWS Glue Workflow, a downstream job should start only after two upstream crawlers have both completed successfully. Which Glue Workflow trigger type supports this multi-predicate, conditional dependency?

choices.text: A scheduled trigger set to run every 5 minutes
A conditional trigger with AND on both crawlers
An on-demand trigger with manual invocation only
Job bookmarks configured on the downstream job

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A conditional trigger with AND logic fires the downstream job only after both crawlers succeed.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Scheduled trigger: ignores dependencies.
• On-demand: manual.
• Bookmarks: incremental data.

Key takeaway: dependencies in Glue workflows → conditional triggers.

stem: An EventBridge rule invokes a Lambda function as part of a pipeline, but occasionally the function fails after exhausting its configured retries, and those failed events are currently lost with no record. Which configuration should be added to preserve failed events for later inspection and reprocessing?

choices.text: Enable S3 Versioning on the pipeline's output bucket
Disable retries on the EventBridge rule
A dead-letter queue on the rule target
Increase the Lambda function's timeout to 15 minutes

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A dead-letter queue (such as SQS) on the EventBridge target captures events that fail after retries.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 versioning: unrelated.
• Disable retries: loses events.
• Longer timeout: doesn't capture failures.

Key takeaway: capture failed events → DLQ.

stem: A company running Amazon MWAA wants the Airflow environment to remain highly available and automatically scale worker capacity as concurrently running tasks increase, without manual intervention. Which statement about MWAA is accurate?

choices.text: MWAA autoscales workers and spans multiple AZs
MWAA only supports a single, fixed number of workers with no autoscaling
MWAA requires manually launching additional EC2 instances to scale workers
MWAA does not support Availability Zone redundancy

explanation:
Why this is correct:
MWAA runs across multiple AZs and automatically scales workers within the configured minimum and maximum.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Fixed workers: it autoscales.
• Manual EC2: no.
• No AZ redundancy: it has it.

Key takeaway: MWAA autoscaling is built in.

stem: A workflow must validate 3,000 files independently in parallel, with a concurrency limit and a failure tolerance of 1%. Which Step Functions feature fits?

choices.text: A Wait state between each file
A Choice state looping over the file list
A Parallel state with 3,000 hard-coded branches
Distributed Map with concurrency and failure limits

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The Map state iterates over items in parallel. Distributed mode scales to large item counts from S3, with concurrency limits and a tolerated failure threshold.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Parallel with 3,000 branches: fixed branches, not dynamic iteration.
• Choice loop: sequential and slow.
• Wait: only delays.

Key takeaway: iterate items in parallel → Map (Distributed for scale).

stem: A team is deciding between AWS Step Functions and Amazon MWAA to orchestrate a pipeline of about 10 steps that runs twice a day. They have no existing Airflow expertise or DAGs and want to minimize both operational overhead and idle infrastructure cost. Which service better fits this situation, and why?

choices.text: Step Functions: serverless, no idle environment cost
MWAA, because it has no minimum environment cost regardless of usage
Step Functions, because it requires Python DAG authoring the team can learn quickly
MWAA, because it is cheaper for infrequent, small workflows with no existing DAGs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
For a small number of infrequent workflows, Step Functions is serverless with no always-on environment cost. MWAA has a minimum environment cost.

Why the other options are wrong:
• MWAA no minimum cost: false.
• Step Functions needs Python DAGs: no.
• MWAA cheaper for small workflows: no.

Key takeaway: light orchestration → Step Functions.

stem: A failed Step Functions execution must be diagnosed: which state failed, its input and output, and the error. Where is this fastest?

choices.text: AWS Config timeline for the state machine
CloudTrail event history for StartExecution
Cost Explorer for the workflow's charges
The execution's event history and graph view

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Step Functions records each state transition with inputs, outputs, and errors, and the console highlights the failed state on the graph.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudTrail: API calls, not state details.
• Config: configuration changes.
• Cost Explorer: billing.

Key takeaway: workflow debugging → execution history.

stem: A completed data pipeline stage needs to notify exactly one downstream processing system to begin the next stage, with guaranteed delivery and the ability for that system to control its own processing rate by polling for the message when ready. Which service is more appropriate than a simple pub/sub push notification?

choices.text: Amazon Pinpoint
Amazon SQS
Legacy CloudWatch Events with no configured target
Amazon SNS without any queue subscriber

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An SQS queue delivers a message to one consumer system, decoupling stages.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Pinpoint: marketing messages.
• Events with no target: nothing happens.
• SNS with no subscriber: nothing delivered.

Key takeaway: notify one consumer reliably → SQS.

stem: A Python-based transformation script processes a large in-memory list using a for-loop with repeated string concatenation, resulting in noticeably slow runtime for large datasets. Which change is most likely to reduce runtime significantly for this specific pattern?

choices.text: Increase the Lambda function's timeout value
Add more print statements to monitor progress
Use vectorized pandas/NumPy or a single join
Switch the code to use recursive function calls

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Vectorized operations (pandas or NumPy) or joins replace slow Python loops over large lists.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Longer timeout: still slow.
• More prints: slower.
• Recursion: slower and risky.

Key takeaway: slow loops → vectorize.

stem: A latency-sensitive ingestion Lambda function suffers from cold-start delays during traffic spikes, causing missed SLAs for the first few invocations after idle periods. Which Lambda configuration most directly addresses cold-start latency?

choices.text: Enabling X-Ray active tracing
Increasing the function's timeout
Reserved concurrency set to 1
Provisioned concurrency

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Provisioned concurrency keeps environments initialized, avoiding cold starts during spikes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• X-Ray: observation.
• Longer timeout: unrelated.
• Reserved concurrency 1: throttles.

Key takeaway: cold starts → provisioned concurrency.

stem: A CPU-bound Lambda transformation function is running slower than expected. Profiling shows the function is single-threaded and CPU-limited rather than I/O-bound. Which configuration change is most likely to improve execution duration?

choices.text: Raise memory, which also raises vCPU
Move the function's code into multiple separate Lambda layers
Decrease the allocated memory to save cost
Increase the function's timeout setting

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Lambda allocates CPU in proportion to memory. Increasing memory gives CPU-bound functions more CPU.

Why the other options are wrong:
• More layers: packaging.
• Less memory: slower.
• Longer timeout: doesn't speed up.

Key takeaway: CPU-bound Lambda → more memory.

stem: A transformation needs custom Python UDFs, iterative feature logic, and joins over 2 TB, which is hard to express in SQL. Which option fits BEST?

choices.text: Athena SQL with nested subqueries
PySpark on Glue or EMR
A single Lambda function in Python
Redshift stored procedures only

explanation:
Why this is correct:
PySpark scales Python logic across a cluster, supports UDFs and complex iterative transforms, and handles terabyte-scale joins.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Athena SQL: awkward for iterative Python logic.
• Single Lambda: memory and time limits.
• Stored procedures: SQL-bound and require loading into Redshift.

Key takeaway: complex Python logic at scale → PySpark.

stem: Engineers overwrite each other's Glue scripts shared by email, with no review or history. Which practice fixes this?

choices.text: A weekly meeting to merge changes manually
Git with branches, pull requests, and CI deployment
Editing scripts only in the Glue console with job versioning
One shared S3 folder with versioning for scripts

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Git provides history, branching, and code review, and CI/CD deploys reviewed scripts to Glue consistently.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 versioning: keeps copies but has no review or merge.
• Console edits: no review.
• Weekly meetings: slow and error-prone.

Key takeaway: treat pipeline code like application code.

stem: A data engineer wants to unit test the transformation logic inside a Glue PySpark job locally without running the actual job against production data or provisioning AWS resources for every test run. Which approach best supports this goal?

choices.text: Extract logic into functions tested locally with pytest
Manually inspect output files in S3 after each deployment
Run the full Glue job against the production Data Catalog for every code change
Disable job bookmarks to speed up testing

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Extracting transformation logic into plain functions lets you unit test them locally (for example, with pytest and a local Spark session) without running the whole Glue job.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Inspect S3 output manually: not unit tests.
• Run against production catalog: risky.
• Disable bookmarks: unrelated.

Key takeaway: testable ETL → separate logic from I/O.

stem: A Glue job fails intermittently. The team must find error patterns across thousands of log lines from many runs and count them by error type. Which tool fits?

choices.text: CloudWatch Logs Insights queries
S3 server access logs
The Glue console's job run list
CloudTrail event history

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Glue writes driver and executor logs to CloudWatch Logs, and Logs Insights can filter and aggregate across runs and streams.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Job run list: status, not log analysis.
• CloudTrail: API calls.
• S3 access logs: bucket requests.

Key takeaway: search and aggregate logs → Logs Insights.

stem: A team wants pipeline infrastructure (buckets, Glue jobs, IAM roles) defined in Python with reusable components and unit tests, deployed via CloudFormation. Which tool fits?

choices.text: AWS Config rules
Systems Manager Parameter Store
AWS Service Catalog
AWS CDK

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The CDK lets you write infrastructure in Python with constructs and tests, then synthesizes CloudFormation.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Config: compliance.
• Service Catalog: distributes products.
• Parameter Store: configuration values.

Key takeaway: IaC in a programming language → CDK.

stem: An ingestion API (API Gateway, Lambda, DynamoDB) must be defined concisely, tested locally, and deployed with gradual Lambda traffic shifting. Which framework fits?

choices.text: Elastic Beanstalk
AWS SAM
AWS OpsWorks
AWS Config

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SAM offers shorthand serverless resources, local testing (sam local), and built-in gradual deployments with CodeDeploy (DeploymentPreference).

Why the other options are wrong:
• OpsWorks: configuration management.
• Config: compliance.
• Beanstalk: web apps on instances.

Key takeaway: serverless apps → SAM.

stem: A Lambda-based transformation function needs to read and write a large shared reference dataset of several GB that exceeds the /tmp ephemeral storage limit and must persist and be shared across concurrent function invocations. Which storage option should be mounted to the function?

choices.text: Only the default /tmp ephemeral storage, increased to its maximum
Instance store volumes on the underlying EC2 host
Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive
An EFS file system mounted by Lambda

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An EFS file system mounted via Lambda's file system configuration provides shared, persistent, read-write storage across invocations.

Why the other options are wrong:
• /tmp only: per environment, not shared.
• Instance store: not accessible.
• Deep Archive: slow.

Key takeaway: shared Lambda file storage → EFS.

stem: A team wants changes to their AWS Glue ETL scripts to be automatically tested and deployed to a staging environment whenever a pull request is merged into the main branch, without manual console uploads. Which combination of services best implements this CI/CD pipeline on AWS?

choices.text: Manually uploading scripts to S3 after each merge
CodePipeline with CodeBuild tests and deploys
Amazon Macie scanning each pull request
AWS Config rules triggered on each git commit

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CodePipeline orchestrating CodeBuild to run tests and deploy scripts automates Glue ETL CI/CD.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Manual uploads: no automation.
• Macie: data scanning.
• Config rules on commits: no.

Key takeaway: ETL CI/CD → CodePipeline + CodeBuild.

stem: During a large Spark join operation on an AWS Glue job, data must be redistributed across the cluster so that records with matching keys end up on the same executor. This network-intensive redistribution process is best known as which distributed computing concept?

choices.text: Checkpointing
Garbage collection
Broadcast variable
Shuffle

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A shuffle redistributes data across partitions (for example, by join key) during wide operations like joins.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Checkpointing: state saving.
• Garbage collection: memory.
• Broadcast: avoids shuffles for small tables.

Key takeaway: joins across partitions → shuffle.

stem: A streaming deduplication component must quickly check whether a record's unique ID has already been seen among millions of prior IDs, prioritizing fast average-case lookup time. Which data structure is most appropriate for this membership-check use case?

choices.text: An unbalanced binary tree traversed depth-first each time
A sorted array requiring linear scan
A hash set or hash-based lookup structure
A singly linked list traversed sequentially

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A hash set gives average constant-time membership checks for record IDs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Unbalanced tree: slow.
• Sorted array linear scan: slow.
• Linked list: slow.

Key takeaway: fast lookups → hash structures.

stem: A Lambda-based ingestion function occasionally receives the same S3 event notification more than once due to at-least-once delivery semantics, and each invocation currently appends a new row to a downstream table, resulting in duplicate records. Which software engineering principle should the function's logic apply to prevent duplicates?

choices.text: Increasing the function's reserved concurrency
Reducing the S3 event notification's payload size
Idempotency keyed on the object's ID
Statelessness only, with no additional logic

explanation:
Why this is correct:
S3 events can be delivered more than once. Idempotent processing (for example, recording processed object keys or version IDs) prevents duplicate effects.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Reserved concurrency: doesn't dedupe.
• Smaller payload: no.
• Stateless only: doesn't prevent duplicates.

Key takeaway: at-least-once events → idempotency.

stem: A script on a Windows EC2 instance must move files between local folders and S3 each night using AWS cmdlets. Which scripting language fits natively?

choices.text: SQL scripts run by the instance
Bash scripts run directly by the Windows command shell
JSON documents executed by the OS
PowerShell with AWS Tools for PowerShell

explanation:
Why this is correct:
PowerShell is native to Windows, and AWS Tools for PowerShell provide S3 cmdlets.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Bash: not native on Windows.
• SQL: queries databases.
• JSON: data, not scripts.

Key takeaway: Windows automation → PowerShell.

stem: Analysts need complex SQL joins and aggregations over billions of rows with concurrency for 200 users and consistent performance. Which store fits?

choices.text: Amazon DynamoDB
Amazon RDS for MySQL
Amazon ElastiCache
Amazon Redshift

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Redshift is a columnar MPP data warehouse designed for large analytical queries, with features such as concurrency scaling.

Why the other options are wrong:
• DynamoDB: key-value access, not complex SQL.
• ElastiCache: in-memory cache.
• RDS MySQL: OLTP, not billions-row analytics.

Key takeaway: analytics at scale → data warehouse.

stem: A gaming application needs a durable key-value store for player session data with microsecond read latency and single-digit millisecond write latency, Redis API compatibility, and data persistence across restarts. Which service best meets this need?

choices.text: Amazon DynamoDB with DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX)
Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached
Amazon MemoryDB for Redis
Amazon Aurora Serverless v2

explanation:
Why this is correct:
MemoryDB for Redis is a durable in-memory database with microsecond reads and Multi-AZ durability.

Why the other options are wrong:
• DynamoDB + DAX: microsecond reads, but writes aren't in-memory latency.
• Memcached: not durable.
• Aurora: not microsecond.

Key takeaway: durable in-memory key-value → MemoryDB.

stem: A team already has Apache Kafka producers and consumers using native Kafka client libraries and protocol. They want to move ingestion to a managed AWS service while keeping full compatibility with existing Kafka APIs and clients. Which service should they choose?

choices.text: Amazon SQS
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams
Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose
Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka (MSK)

explanation:
Why this is correct:
MSK runs Apache Kafka, so existing native Kafka clients work without code changes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SQS, Kinesis, Firehose: different APIs.

Key takeaway: existing Kafka clients → MSK.

stem: A data engineer is building a similarity search feature on Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL storing millions of embedding vectors and needs the fastest approximate nearest neighbor query performance, and can accept longer index build time and higher memory usage in exchange. Which pgvector index type should be selected?

choices.text: Hash index
HNSW index
GIN index
B-tree index

explanation:
Why this is correct:
pgvector's HNSW index enables fast approximate nearest-neighbor similarity search on embeddings.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Hash, GIN, B-tree: not vector similarity indexes.

Key takeaway: vector similarity in Aurora → HNSW.

stem: Which statement correctly describes the primary tradeoff between HNSW and IVF (inverted file) vector index types used for approximate nearest neighbor search?

choices.text: IVF needs a training step; HNSW uses more memory
IVF supports only exact nearest neighbor search
HNSW builds faster and uses less memory than IVF, but always returns lower recall
HNSW and IVF have identical build time, memory usage, and query performance characteristics

explanation:
Why this is correct:
IVF needs a training (clustering) step before indexing and is lighter on memory. HNSW builds a graph with better recall and query speed but uses more memory.

Why the other options are wrong:
• IVF exact only: it's approximate.
• HNSW builds faster with less memory: generally the opposite.
• Identical: no.

Key takeaway: HNSW = recall/speed; IVF = lighter, needs training.

stem: Partners must upload files by SFTP into S3 with their existing keys, and each partner may see only its own folder. No servers should be managed. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS DataSync agents at each partner
Transfer Family SFTP with scoped home folders
S3 presigned URLs emailed daily
An EC2 SFTP server syncing to S3

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Transfer Family provides managed SFTP endpoints backed by S3, with users mapped to scoped IAM roles and logical home directories.

Why the other options are wrong:
• EC2 SFTP: servers to run.
• Presigned URLs: not SFTP.
• DataSync agents: not a partner SFTP service.

Key takeaway: managed SFTP into S3 → Transfer Family.

stem: An analytics team wants to run a single Amazon Redshift SQL query that joins a table already in the Redshift cluster with live operational data still stored in Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL, without first copying that data into Redshift. Which capability enables this?

choices.text: Redshift Spectrum
Redshift federated query
Redshift materialized views
Amazon Athena

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Redshift federated query joins Redshift tables with live data in RDS or Aurora PostgreSQL/MySQL in one query.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Spectrum: S3.
• Materialized views: precomputed.
• Athena: separate engine.

Key takeaway: query operational DBs from Redshift → federated query.

stem: A dashboard runs the same heavy aggregation on a Redshift fact table every minute, and the base table changes a few times per hour. Which feature fits BEST?

choices.text: A UNLOAD of the table to S3 each minute
Result caching disabled to force fresh results
A materialized view with auto refresh
A bigger cluster to run the query faster

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Materialized views store precomputed results and can refresh incrementally (auto refresh), so dashboards read small precomputed data instead of re-aggregating.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Disabling the cache: more work.
• Bigger cluster: costs more for repeated work.
• UNLOAD each minute: wasteful and not a query speedup.

Key takeaway: repeated heavy aggregation → materialized views.

stem: A data engineer needs to query historical Parquet files stored in Amazon S3 directly from Redshift SQL, joining them with local Redshift tables, without loading the files into the cluster. Which feature should be used?

choices.text: Redshift federated query
Redshift Spectrum
AWS Glue crawler
Amazon Athena federated query

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Redshift Spectrum queries Parquet files in S3 directly through external tables.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Federated query: operational databases.
• Glue crawler: cataloging.
• Athena federated query: separate engine.

Key takeaway: S3 data from Redshift → Spectrum.

stem: An ETL job running VACUUM on a Redshift table hangs, and a concurrent COPY into the same table, along with other sessions trying to query it, are all blocked. What is the most likely cause and correct troubleshooting action?

choices.text: A long transaction holds a lock; find and terminate it
The table has exceeded its maximum row count; increase the cluster's node count
The WLM queue has zero concurrency slots configured; disable WLM entirely to resolve it
Redshift automatically resolves all lock contention within 30 seconds, so no action is needed

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A long-running open transaction holding a lock blocks VACUUM and COPY. Find it in the system tables (such as STV_LOCKS) and end it.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Max rows: no.
• WLM zero slots: not the symptom.
• Auto-resolved: no.

Key takeaway: hanging Redshift jobs → lock contention.

stem: A data lake team needs ACID transactions, schema evolution, and time-travel queries on datasets stored as files in Amazon S3, while remaining queryable by multiple engines such as Athena, EMR Spark, and Redshift Spectrum. Which open table format addresses these requirements?

choices.text: Apache Parquet
Apache ORC
Apache Iceberg
Delimited CSV with manifest files

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Apache Iceberg adds ACID transactions, schema evolution, and time travel to data lake tables.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Parquet and ORC: file formats only.
• CSV with manifests: no ACID.

Key takeaway: transactional data lake tables → Iceberg.

stem: An application must retrieve all orders for a given customer, sorted by order date, using a single efficient DynamoDB query. How should the table's key schema be designed to support this access pattern?

choices.text: Partition key = CustomerID, sort key = OrderDate
Partition key = OrderID, no sort key
Partition key = OrderDate, sort key = CustomerID
Partition key = a random UUID, sort key = OrderID

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Partition key CustomerID with sort key OrderDate lets one Query return a customer's orders sorted by date.

Why the other options are wrong:
• OrderID only: can't query by customer.
• Date as partition: wrong grouping.
• Random UUID: no access pattern.

Key takeaway: design keys for the access pattern.

stem: A team needs Spark and Hive with specific open-source versions and custom bootstrap actions, on a cluster it can tune. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Glue with its default settings
Amazon Athena SQL
AWS Batch with a generic container
Amazon EMR

explanation:
Why this is correct:
EMR offers control over open-source application versions, configuration, and bootstrap actions for Spark, Hive, and more.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Glue: managed Spark with less control over versions and cluster tuning.
• Athena: SQL only.
• Batch: generic jobs; you'd install and manage Spark yourself.

Key takeaway: control over big-data frameworks → EMR.

stem: A company's Glue Data Catalog tables point to data in S3, and the company wants to enforce fine-grained, column-level and row-level access permissions on those tables for different analyst groups querying through both Athena and Redshift Spectrum. Which service should be used to define and enforce these permissions?

choices.text: AWS Glue crawlers
AWS Lake Formation
IAM policies applied directly to the S3 bucket only
Amazon Macie

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Lake Formation enforces fine-grained table, column, and row permissions on data cataloged in Glue.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Crawlers: discovery.
• S3 IAM only: no column-level control.
• Macie: discovery.

Key takeaway: fine-grained data lake permissions → Lake Formation.

stem: Athena, EMR, Redshift Spectrum, and Glue jobs all need the same table definitions for S3 data. What provides this?

choices.text: S3 object tags describing each column
The Glue Data Catalog as a shared metastore
A README file in each bucket prefix
Each engine keeping its own local metastore

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The Glue Data Catalog stores databases, tables, schemas, and locations, and is used by Athena, EMR (as a Hive metastore), Redshift Spectrum, and Glue.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Local metastores: definitions diverge.
• Object tags: not schemas.
• README files: not machine-readable metadata.

Key takeaway: one catalog for many engines → Glue Data Catalog.

stem: A company migrating an on-premises Hadoop/Hive environment to AWS wants its existing EMR Hive and Spark jobs, which rely on the Hive metastore API, to work with minimal code changes while sharing a managed, centrally accessible catalog across clusters. What should they configure?

choices.text: Replace the metastore with Amazon RDS, requiring a full schema redesign
Rewrite all Hive queries to use DynamoDB as the metadata store
Use the Glue Data Catalog as EMR's Hive metastore
Store metadata only in each EMR cluster's local Hive metastore, with no central sharing

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Configuring EMR to use the Glue Data Catalog as its external Hive metastore keeps metadata persistent and shared across clusters and services.

Why the other options are wrong:
• RDS metastore rewrite: unnecessary.
• DynamoDB metadata: no.
• Local metastore: lost with clusters.

Key takeaway: shared Hive metastore → Glue Data Catalog.

stem: Raw JSON with an evolving schema lands daily. Tables must appear in Athena automatically, and new fields should be added without breaking queries. Which feature fits?

choices.text: A Lambda function that edits the table DDL by hand
Athena CTAS each morning to rebuild the table
A scheduled Glue crawler with a schema update policy
A Glue ETL job that deletes and recreates tables

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Crawlers infer schemas, including nested JSON, and their schema change policy controls how new columns are added to existing tables.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Recreating tables: breaks consumers.
• Daily CTAS: rewrites data unnecessarily.
• Manual DDL edits: fragile.

Key takeaway: schema discovery → crawlers.

stem: New daily partitions are being written to S3 under a Hive-style partitioned path, but Athena queries filtering on recent dates return no results for the newest partitions even though the files exist in S3. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: S3 bucket versioning is disabled, which prevents new object reads
The IAM role used by Athena has been deleted
The partitions aren't registered in the Glue catalog yet
Athena does not support partitioned tables

explanation:
Why this is correct:
New partitions must be registered in the Glue Data Catalog (via crawler, MSCK REPAIR, ALTER TABLE, or partition projection) before Athena sees them.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Versioning: unrelated.
• Deleted role: would fail entirely.
• Athena doesn't support partitions: it does.

Key takeaway: new partitions → register or use projection.

stem: Business users must find curated datasets using business terms, see ownership and quality, and request access that owners approve. Which service fits?

choices.text: The Glue Data Catalog console alone
AWS Config resource inventory with tags
Amazon SageMaker Catalog (DataZone-based)
An S3 bucket listing in the console

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SageMaker Catalog (built on DataZone) provides business glossary, metadata, search, and publish-subscribe access workflows for governed data sharing.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Glue catalog alone: technical metadata without business workflows.
• Config: resource inventory.
• Bucket listing: no metadata or requests.

Key takeaway: business data discovery and access requests → SageMaker Catalog.

stem: A Glue crawler run over the same S3 folder repeatedly creates new table versions with slightly different inferred column data types, causing downstream Athena queries to intermittently fail with type-mismatch errors. What is a likely cause and fix?

choices.text: This is expected default behavior and cannot be changed or mitigated
Classifiers infer varying schemas; standardize files and settings
Athena does not support schema versioning
The issue is caused by S3 bucket versioning and can only be fixed by disabling it

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Classifiers inferring slightly different schemas create new table versions. Configure the crawler's schema change policy or custom classifiers.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Can't change: configurable.
• Athena doesn't support versioning: unrelated.
• S3 versioning: unrelated.

Key takeaway: schema flapping → crawler configuration.

stem: A table's underlying S3 data changes only once per month, but a Glue crawler is currently scheduled to run every hour against it. What is the main drawback of this configuration?

choices.text: AWS requires all crawlers to run hourly regardless of data change frequency
Crawlers cannot be scheduled less frequently than hourly
There is no drawback, since crawler runs incur no charges
Needless runs add crawler cost without new schema info
Hourly crawling automatically deletes the table if no changes are found

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Crawling hourly when data changes monthly incurs unnecessary crawler charges. Schedule to match the data or trigger on change.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Required hourly: no.
• Can't schedule less: can.
• No charges: they're charged.
• Deletes table: no.

Key takeaway: match crawler schedule to data changes.

stem: A company wants to grant a data science team read-only access to specific tables and columns already registered in the Glue Data Catalog, enforced consistently whether the team queries through Athena or Redshift Spectrum. What is the recommended approach?

choices.text: Manually copy the S3 bucket policies to a second bucket dedicated to the data science team
Create a separate Glue Data Catalog for the data science team and duplicate the metadata
Register in Lake Formation and grant table/column access
Grant the data science team full S3 bucket-level IAM access

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Registering the data in Lake Formation and granting table and column permissions gives read-only access to exactly what's needed.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Copy bucket policies: no column control.
• Separate catalog: duplication.
• Full bucket access: over-privileged.

Key takeaway: table/column access → Lake Formation grants.

stem: A daily job must export a Redshift query result to S3 as Parquet, partitioned by date, in parallel. Which command fits?

choices.text: INSERT INTO an external table only
A SELECT run from the query editor with results downloaded
UNLOAD with FORMAT PARQUET and PARTITION BY
COPY with FORMAT PARQUET

explanation:
Why this is correct:
UNLOAD writes query results to S3 in parallel, supports Parquet, and can partition output by columns.

Why the other options are wrong:
• COPY: loads data into Redshift.
• External table insert: possible in some cases but not the standard export tool described.
• Query editor: not an export mechanism.

Key takeaway: export from Redshift → UNLOAD; load → COPY.

stem: Several gzip CSV files in S3 must be loaded into a Redshift table quickly using all slices. Which approach fits?

choices.text: COPY from many split files
One huge single file loaded by COPY
UNLOAD from S3 into the table
Individual INSERT statements for each row

explanation:
Why this is correct:
COPY loads in parallel across slices. Splitting data into multiple files (ideally a multiple of the slice count) maximizes parallelism.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Row INSERTs: very slow.
• One huge file: limits parallelism.
• UNLOAD: exports, not loads.

Key takeaway: bulk load → COPY from many files.

stem: A company retains log files that are accessed frequently for 30 days, occasionally for the following 60 days, and must be kept for 7 years for compliance but is almost never accessed after 90 days. Which S3 feature should be configured to automatically move objects between storage classes over time and minimize cost?

choices.text: S3 Object Lock
S3 Transfer Acceleration
S3 Cross-Region Replication
An S3 Lifecycle policy with transition rules

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An S3 Lifecycle policy with transitions moves logs to cheaper classes as access declines, and can expire them later.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Object Lock: retention.
• Transfer Acceleration: speed.
• CRR: replication.

Key takeaway: declining access → lifecycle transitions.

stem: A DynamoDB table stores sessions that must disappear 24 hours after creation, without consuming write capacity for deletes, and deletions must be archived to S3. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Switching the table to on-demand capacity
A scheduled Lambda that scans and deletes items
A GSI keyed on the creation timestamp for expired items
TTL, with Streams capturing expirations for archive

explanation:
Why this is correct:
TTL deletes expired items without consuming write capacity. Those deletions appear in DynamoDB Streams, where Lambda can archive them to S3.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Scan and delete: consumes capacity and costs more.
• On-demand: billing mode only.
• GSI: doesn't delete anything.

Key takeaway: automatic expiry → TTL; archive via Streams.

stem: A compliance requirement states that if an object in an S3 bucket is accidentally overwritten or deleted, the previous version must still be recoverable. Which S3 feature directly satisfies this requirement?

choices.text: S3 Transfer Acceleration
S3 Intelligent-Tiering
S3 Requester Pays
S3 Versioning

explanation:
Why this is correct:
S3 Versioning keeps previous versions, so overwritten objects can be recovered.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Transfer Acceleration, Intelligent-Tiering, Requester Pays: unrelated.

Key takeaway: recover overwrites → versioning.

stem: A company must permanently delete a customer's data from an S3 bucket that has both Versioning and Object Lock enabled in Compliance mode, to satisfy a right-to-erasure request, but discovers the objects cannot be deleted before their retention period expires. What is the correct explanation?

choices.text: Object Lock only applies to the current version
Compliance mode blocks deletion by anyone until retention ends
Enabling Versioning automatically disables Object Lock restrictions for compliance-driven deletions
Compliance mode can always be bypassed by an IAM administrator granted s3:BypassGovernanceRetention permission

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Object Lock in Compliance mode prevents deletion or overwriting of locked versions until retention expires, even by administrators. The data can't be deleted early.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Current version only: applies per version.
• Versioning disables Object Lock: no.
• Admins can bypass: not in compliance mode.

Key takeaway: compliance mode is absolute until expiry.

stem: A team is exporting a very large Redshift query result set to S3 for downstream consumption by Amazon Athena. Which UNLOAD configuration choice most directly improves both export throughput and the performance of subsequent Athena queries against the exported data?

choices.text: Unloading to a single uncompressed CSV file
Parallel UNLOAD to compressed Parquet files
Disabling compression entirely to reduce leader node CPU usage
Using individual INSERT statements from a Lambda function to write rows one at a time into S3

explanation:
Why this is correct:
UNLOAD with parallel output (the default) and a columnar format such as Parquet writes multiple files quickly and efficiently for downstream use.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Single CSV: slow.
• Disable compression: larger output.
• Lambda INSERTs: impractical.

Key takeaway: large exports → parallel UNLOAD to Parquet.

stem: A financial services company must ensure that critical datasets in an S3 bucket remain available and recoverable even if an entire AWS Region becomes unavailable. Which feature should be configured to protect against this scenario?

choices.text: S3 Same-Region Replication (SRR)
S3 Lifecycle expiration
S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR)
S3 Select

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Cross-Region Replication keeps copies in another Region, so data stays available during a Regional outage.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SRR: same Region.
• Expiration: deletes.
• S3 Select: queries.

Key takeaway: Regional resilience → CRR.

stem: To protect a Redshift cluster's data against accidental table corruption and enable point-in-time restoration to a new cluster, which native Redshift capability should be relied upon?

choices.text: Materialized views
Automated and manual snapshots
Concurrency scaling
Redshift Spectrum

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Automated and manual snapshots let you restore a Redshift cluster or table to a previous point.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Materialized views: performance.
• Concurrency scaling: performance.
• Spectrum: S3 queries.

Key takeaway: Redshift recovery → snapshots.

stem: After enabling an S3 Lifecycle rule that transitions objects to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 30 days, a team notices that many small objects, only a few KB each, now cost more in overhead than before the transition, despite the lower per-GB Glacier price. What is the most likely explanation?

choices.text: S3 Glacier Deep Archive charges no fees regardless of object size, so this cannot happen
Each transition has per-object overhead costing more
S3 Lifecycle rules cannot be applied to objects smaller than 128 KB
Small objects are automatically deleted instead of transitioned

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Each object transitioned to a Glacier class incurs a per-object transition charge, plus per-object metadata overhead, so many small objects can cost more.

Why the other options are wrong:
• No fees: false.
• Can't apply to small objects: false.
• Small objects deleted: false.

Key takeaway: lifecycle transitions cost per object.

stem: A team needs the ability to restore a DynamoDB table to any point in time within the last 35 days after an application bug caused unwanted writes, without needing to manually schedule backups. Which feature should be enabled?

choices.text: DynamoDB Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR)
DynamoDB on-demand backup only
DynamoDB Streams
DynamoDB Global Tables

explanation:
Why this is correct:
DynamoDB Point-in-Time Recovery restores to any second within the last 35 days.

Why the other options are wrong:
• On-demand backups only: fixed points.
• Streams: 24-hour change log.
• Global Tables: replication.

Key takeaway: any-point restore → PITR.

stem: A versioning-enabled S3 bucket has a Lifecycle rule that expires the current version of objects after 90 days, but has no rule covering noncurrent versions. What is the consequence of this configuration over time?

choices.text: The bucket automatically disables versioning once the first object expires
Versioned buckets ignore Lifecycle expiration rules entirely
Expiring the current version automatically deletes all noncurrent versions as well, keeping storage flat
A delete marker is added; noncurrent versions remain

explanation:
Why this is correct:
In a versioned bucket, expiring the current version adds a delete marker; the previous version becomes noncurrent and remains unless a noncurrent expiration rule removes it.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Disables versioning: no.
• Ignores rules: no.
• Deletes all versions: no.

Key takeaway: versioned expiration → delete markers + noncurrent versions.

stem: A large Redshift fact table is frequently joined to a dimension table on customer_id, and queries commonly filter and aggregate by order_date. Which combination of schema design choices would most improve query performance?

choices.text: Set the sort key to customer_id and leave distribution style as EVEN for both tables
Set the sort key to a column never used in WHERE clauses and choose ALL distribution style for the large fact table
DISTKEY customer_id for collocated joins; SORTKEY order_date
Avoid setting any distribution or sort keys so Redshift decides automatically at query time

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Setting the distribution key to customer_id on both tables co-locates joined rows on the same slices, avoiding data redistribution.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Sort key only: doesn't collocate.
• Unused sort key: no benefit.
• No keys: may redistribute.

Key takeaway: frequent joins → matching distribution keys.

stem: When designing tables that will be governed by AWS Lake Formation for a multi-tenant data lake, which practice best supports enforcing column-level security for sensitive fields such as national ID numbers?

choices.text: Store sensitive and non-sensitive columns in the same table with no separation, relying only on application-level filtering
Encrypt the entire table with a single shared KMS key and grant all users decrypt permission
Store all sensitive data in a separate AWS account with no catalog entry at all
Identify sensitive columns and use Lake Formation filters

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Defining clear, well-organized schemas in the Glue Data Catalog (with sensitive columns identifiable, and tags if needed) lets Lake Formation apply column-level and tag-based permissions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Mixing sensitive columns without structure: harder to govern.
• Single shared key: no fine-grained control.
• Separate account with no access model: impractical.

Key takeaway: governable schemas enable fine-grained control.
