stem: A DynamoDB table originally designed with a partition key of order_status, a low-cardinality attribute with only four possible values, is now experiencing hot-partition throttling as write volume has grown substantially. What is the most appropriate schema-level fix to address this changed data characteristic?

choices.text: Use a higher-cardinality key or write sharding
Add a global secondary index using the same order_status partition key to double the write capacity
Reduce the table's read capacity to free up more write capacity
Switch the table's billing mode from on-demand to provisioned to eliminate throttling

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A low-cardinality partition key concentrates traffic. Redesign with a higher-cardinality key (for example, order ID or composite keys).

Why the other options are wrong:
• GSI with same key: same hot spot.
• Reduce reads: unrelated.
• Billing mode switch: doesn't fix hot keys.

Key takeaway: hot partitions → higher-cardinality keys.

stem: An Oracle data warehouse moving to Redshift has PL/SQL procedures and Oracle-specific types that must be converted, with a report on items needing manual work. Which tool fits?

choices.text: AWS Glue crawlers over the Oracle schemas
Redshift COPY commands
AWS DMS full load alone
AWS SCT (or DMS Schema Conversion)

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Schema conversion tools convert schemas and code between engines and produce an assessment report of objects needing manual effort. DMS then moves the data.

Why the other options are wrong:
• DMS alone: moves data, not code conversion.
• Crawlers: catalog schemas.
• COPY: loads data.

Key takeaway: heterogeneous schema/code conversion → SCT or DMS Schema Conversion.

stem: A team wants schema conversion and data migration handled within a single managed AWS Database Migration Service project, using DMS's built-in schema conversion capability instead of a separately installed desktop application. Which statement accurately compares this option to using the standalone AWS Schema Conversion Tool (SCT)?

choices.text: DMS Schema Conversion is built into DMS; SCT is installed
DMS Schema Conversion and SCT are entirely unrelated tools with no shared capability
SCT can migrate live data
DMS Schema Conversion only supports migrations where the source and target are the same database engine

explanation:
Why this is correct:
DMS Schema Conversion is a managed, console-integrated feature for converting schemas within DMS, alongside data migration.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Unrelated tools: they overlap.
• SCT migrates live data: DMS does.
• Same-engine only: supports heterogeneous.

Key takeaway: schema + data in DMS → DMS Schema Conversion.

stem: Auditors ask which dataset version, processing job, and training job produced a deployed model, and which endpoints use it. Which capability fits?

choices.text: CloudTrail event history
SageMaker ML Lineage Tracking
S3 Inventory reports on the model artifact bucket
AWS Config timeline

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Lineage Tracking records entities (datasets, jobs, models, endpoints) and their relationships, so you can trace a model back to its inputs and forward to deployments.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudTrail: API calls without artifact relationships.
• S3 Inventory: object lists.
• Config: resource configuration.

Key takeaway: artifact relationships → Lineage Tracking.

stem: A governance team wants business users browsing Amazon SageMaker Catalog to see not just a dataset's schema, but also which upstream sources and transformation jobs produced it. What underlying capability supports surfacing this lineage information within the catalog experience?

choices.text: SageMaker Catalog can only show column names and data types, with no lineage information available
Lineage information must be manually re-entered as free-text notes with no system linkage
Lineage can only be viewed through raw Glue Data Catalog table properties, never through SageMaker Catalog
It surfaces lineage alongside business metadata

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SageMaker Catalog integrates with lineage tracking, so business users can see where data came from and how it was transformed, not just its schema.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Only names and types: it shows more.
• Manual free-text lineage: no.
• Only raw Glue views: no.

Key takeaway: trust in data → surface lineage in the catalog.

stem: A data lake table stored as Parquet in S3 is queried through Athena almost always with a filter on the event_date column, and the table has grown to hundreds of millions of rows. Which design change would most reduce the amount of data scanned, and therefore cost and latency, per query?

choices.text: Add a global secondary index to the S3 bucket
Merge all files into a single very large file regardless of date
Partition by event_date so Athena prunes partitions
Convert the files from Parquet to uncompressed CSV

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Partitioning the data and table by event_date lets Athena skip files outside the filter, scanning less data.

Why the other options are wrong:
• GSI on S3: doesn't exist.
• One huge file: hurts parallelism.
• Uncompressed CSV: slower.

Key takeaway: frequent date filters → partition by date.

stem: A Redshift table was created without explicit column encoding, resulting in larger-than-necessary disk usage and slower scan performance. What is the recommended way to improve storage efficiency and query performance for this table?

choices.text: Apply suitable column encodings (ANALYZE COMPRESSION)
Increase the cluster's node count without changing the table's encoding
Convert the table into a view to avoid storing any data on disk
Disable compression entirely

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Applying suitable column encodings (for example, AZ64 or ZSTD, or ENCODE AUTO) shrinks storage and I/O, speeding queries.

Why the other options are wrong:
• More nodes: costs more without fixing encoding.
• Convert to view: no storage.
• Disable compression: worse.

Key takeaway: Redshift storage → column encodings.

stem: Which statement correctly contrasts the role of a Redshift sort key with a DynamoDB Global Secondary Index (GSI)?

choices.text: Sort keys order data on disk; GSIs add query patterns
Both serve identical purposes; they are the same mechanism with different names across services
A DynamoDB GSI physically reorders the base table's items on disk, exactly like a Redshift sort key
A Redshift sort key can be added or changed at query time with no effect on stored data layout, just like a DynamoDB GSI

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A Redshift sort key physically orders data on disk so zone maps skip blocks. A DynamoDB GSI is a separate index with its own keys for a different access pattern.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Identical: no.
• GSI reorders base table: no.
• Sort key changed at query time: no.

Key takeaway: sort key = physical order; GSI = alternate access path.

stem: A RAG app's knowledge base returns irrelevant chunks for questions phrased differently from the documents' wording. What role does the embedding model play, and what fixes this?

choices.text: It generates the final answer; a larger LLM fixes this
It compresses documents for storage; more compression fixes this
It translates queries; turning translation off fixes this
It maps text to vectors for semantic search; choose a suitable one

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Embeddings represent meaning as vectors so similar meanings are close even with different wording. Choosing a domain-appropriate embedding model (and good chunking) improves retrieval.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Answer generation: that's the LLM, not the embedding model.
• Compression: not the role.
• Translation: not the role.

Key takeaway: retrieval quality depends on embeddings and chunking.

stem: A team is designing a DynamoDB schema for an e-commerce order system and is deciding between normalizing data, using separate items requiring multiple queries to assemble an order view, versus denormalizing, such as embedding product details within each order item. What is the primary tradeoff of choosing denormalization in DynamoDB?

choices.text: Denormalization only affects write costs and has no impact on read patterns
Denormalization has no downsides in DynamoDB and should always be preferred over normalization
Faster reads, at the cost of duplicated data to keep in sync
Denormalization is not possible in DynamoDB

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Denormalization stores related data together for fast single-request reads, at the cost of duplicated data and more complex updates.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Only affects writes: affects reads too.
• No downsides: there are.
• Not possible: common practice.

Key takeaway: DynamoDB denormalization trades update complexity for read speed.

stem: A workflow runs Glue jobs, an EMR step, and Lambda, with conditional branches, retries, and waits for completion, and must be visualized for operators. Which fits?

choices.text: A single Glue trigger
A cron job on an EC2 instance
An EventBridge rule per step
AWS Step Functions

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Step Functions integrates with Glue, EMR, and Lambda (including run-to-completion patterns), supports branching and retries, and shows each execution visually.

Why the other options are wrong:
• EventBridge rules per step: event wiring without workflow state.
• Glue trigger: limited to Glue.
• EC2 cron: custom logic and servers.

Key takeaway: cross-service workflows with state → Step Functions.

stem: Tasks in an Amazon MWAA environment are remaining in the queued state for a long time before executing, even though the DAG code has no bugs and the scheduler shows no errors. Which configuration change is most likely to resolve this?

choices.text: Enable versioning on the MWAA environment's S3 bucket
Decrease the DAG's schedule_interval
Raise the environment class or max workers
Change the DAG's start_date to an earlier date

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Queued tasks mean there aren't enough workers. Increase the environment class or maximum worker count.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 versioning: unrelated.
• Shorter schedule: more load.
• Earlier start_date: backfills more.

Key takeaway: queued Airflow tasks → more worker capacity.

stem: A Python Lambda function must start a Glue job with runtime arguments whenever a message arrives, and record the run ID. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Invoke the Glue job through its S3 script URL
Use CloudFormation to create a new job each time
Call glue.start_job_run() with Boto3
Put the arguments in an SNS topic for Glue

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The Boto3 Glue client's start_job_run accepts the job name and arguments and returns a JobRunId.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 script URL: not an invocation method.
• SNS to Glue: Glue doesn't subscribe to SNS.
• Creating jobs per run: unnecessary.

Key takeaway: call AWS services from code via the SDK.

stem: A pipeline needs to pull data every hour from a third-party REST API that returns results across multiple pages, using a nextToken field in the JSON response to indicate more pages exist. Which approach correctly handles this inside a Lambda-based ingestion function?

choices.text: Configure Amazon API Gateway to automatically merge the third-party API's paginated responses
Increase the Lambda function's timeout
Loop, passing nextToken until none is returned
Make a single API call and assume all data is returned in that one response

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Paginated APIs require looping and passing the returned nextToken until no token remains.

Why the other options are wrong:
• API Gateway merging: no.
• Longer timeout: doesn't stop pagination.
• Single call: misses data.

Key takeaway: paginated APIs → loop on nextToken.

stem: Before building a pipeline, an engineer wants to profile a new dataset visually (nulls, distributions, outliers) and try cleaning steps without code. Which tool fits?

choices.text: Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose
Amazon Athena
AWS Glue DataBrew
AWS Glue crawler

explanation:
Why this is correct:
DataBrew provides visual data profiling and 250+ transformations, saved as recipes that can run as jobs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Crawler: schema only.
• Athena: SQL, no visual profiling.
• Firehose: streaming delivery.

Key takeaway: visual profiling and cleaning → DataBrew.

stem: Data engineers, analysts, and ML engineers want one workspace for SQL, notebooks, data prep, and model building on governed data, with shared projects. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio
Amazon QuickSight
AWS Cloud9 with shared environments
AWS Glue Studio

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SageMaker Unified Studio brings together data processing, SQL analytics, and ML/AI development in project-based collaborative workspaces with governed data access.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Glue Studio: ETL authoring only.
• QuickSight: BI dashboards.
• Cloud9: a general IDE.

Key takeaway: one workspace for data + analytics + AI → Unified Studio.

stem: A data engineer wants to create a new, permanent table in the AWS Glue Data Catalog whose data is the materialized result of a complex Athena SQL query, stored as compressed Parquet files in S3, so downstream jobs can query it efficiently. Which Athena capability should be used?

choices.text: CREATE TABLE AS SELECT (CTAS)
A named query with parameters
A saved query
UNLOAD

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CTAS creates a new permanent table in the Glue Data Catalog from a query's results, with chosen format and location.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Named query: stored SQL text.
• Saved query: stored SQL text.
• UNLOAD: writes files without a table.

Key takeaway: new table from a query → CTAS.

stem: A validation function must run the moment objects are created under incoming/, and a second team also wants the same events without changing the first setup. Which design fits?

choices.text: S3 events to EventBridge, one rule per consumer
The Lambda function polling the bucket
A crawler running every minute over incoming/
CloudTrail Insights on the bucket's write activity

explanation:
Why this is correct:
EventBridge receives S3 object-created events and lets multiple rules route them to independent targets, such as each team's Lambda.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Crawler: catalogs; doesn't trigger validation.
• Polling: delay and cost.
• CloudTrail Insights: anomaly detection.

Key takeaway: multiple consumers of S3 events → EventBridge.

stem: A company wants a Step Functions state machine to start automatically whenever an object matching a specific pattern is created in an S3 bucket, without writing custom polling code. Which combination of services achieves this?

choices.text: Configure the state machine to poll the S3 bucket every 5 minutes using a Wait state
Use AWS Config to detect the change and manually start the execution
S3 EventBridge notifications and a rule targeting the state machine
Create an SNS topic with only an email subscription and manually start the execution when the email arrives

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Enable S3 EventBridge notifications, then create a rule matching the object key pattern that starts the state machine.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Polling every 5 minutes: delayed.
• Config then manual start: slow.
• SNS email: manual.

Key takeaway: S3 events → EventBridge → Step Functions.

stem: Executives need interactive drill-down dashboards, while an engineer must profile and clean raw data visually first. Which pair fits?

choices.text: Athena for both dashboards and profiling
QuickSight for dashboards; DataBrew for profiling
DataBrew for dashboards; QuickSight for profiling
CloudWatch dashboards for executives; Glue crawlers for cleaning

explanation:
Why this is correct:
QuickSight builds interactive BI dashboards. DataBrew profiles and cleans data visually.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Swapped: each tool in the other's role.
• Athena: queries only.
• CloudWatch/crawlers: operational metrics and schema discovery.

Key takeaway: BI → QuickSight; visual data prep → DataBrew.

stem: A data scientist wants to visually explore feature distributions, detect target leakage, and generate a bias report for a dataset intended for ML model training, all within a low-code visual interface, then export the resulting transforms as a reusable pipeline step. Which service is designed specifically for this?

choices.text: AWS Glue DataBrew
Amazon Athena
Amazon QuickSight
Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Data Wrangler provides visual exploration, target leakage detection, and quick model analysis for ML data preparation.

Why the other options are wrong:
• DataBrew: general prep without ML insights.
• Athena: queries.
• QuickSight: dashboards.

Key takeaway: ML data exploration → Data Wrangler.

stem: An engineer wants to run Python cells interactively on a sample, inspect DataFrames, plot results, and document findings for teammates. Which fits?

choices.text: A CloudFormation template
A Lambda function with print statements
A Glue ETL job run on a schedule
A Jupyter notebook in SageMaker Studio

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Notebooks support interactive execution, inline outputs and charts, and documentation cells, which suits exploration and sharing.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Scheduled ETL: not interactive.
• Lambda prints: not exploratory.
• CloudFormation: infrastructure.

Key takeaway: interactive exploration → notebooks.

stem: An analyst runs the following Athena query: SELECT region, SUM(amount) AS total_sales FROM sales GROUP BY region HAVING SUM(amount) > 100000; What does this query return?

choices.text: Only the single region with the highest total sales
An error, because HAVING cannot be used together with an aggregate function like SUM
Each region's total sales, but only for regions whose total sales exceed 100000
Every individual sales row where the amount column exceeds 100000

explanation:
Why this is correct:
GROUP BY region with SUM computes totals per region, and HAVING keeps only regions whose total exceeds the threshold.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Only the highest region: no.
• HAVING with aggregate errors: it's valid.
• Individual rows: HAVING filters groups.

Key takeaway: HAVING filters aggregated groups.

stem: In Amazon Redshift, which SQL construct correctly computes, for each row, a 7-day rolling average of daily_sales ordered by sale_date?

choices.text: AVG(daily_sales) OVER (PARTITION BY sale_date)
SUM(daily_sales) / COUNT(*) with no OVER or GROUP BY clause
AVG(daily_sales) GROUP BY sale_date
AVG() OVER (ORDER BY date ROWS 6 PRECEDING)

explanation:
Why this is correct:
AVG(...) OVER (ORDER BY sale_date ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) computes a 7-day rolling average per row.

Why the other options are wrong:
• PARTITION BY date: averages within each date.
• No OVER: single value.
• GROUP BY date: no rolling window.

Key takeaway: rolling metrics → window frames.

stem: Analysts use Athena SQL but need Python transformations with Spark libraries on the same S3 data, without managing clusters. Which capability fits?

choices.text: Athena SQL user-defined functions only
Athena for Apache Spark notebooks
Redshift Spectrum
A permanent EMR cluster

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Athena for Apache Spark runs PySpark interactively in notebooks within Athena, serverlessly, against data in S3.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SQL UDFs: limited compared to Spark.
• EMR: cluster management.
• Spectrum: SQL from Redshift.

Key takeaway: serverless interactive Spark → Athena for Spark.

stem: A startup's Redshift analytics workload is highly unpredictable: some weeks see almost no queries, while a monthly reporting cycle produces a two-day spike of heavy queries. The team wants to minimize cost during idle periods while still handling the spike, without manually resizing clusters. Which approach best fits this pattern?

choices.text: A single fixed-size provisioned Redshift cluster sized for the monthly peak, running continuously
Redshift Serverless, which scales and bills by usage
A provisioned Redshift cluster paused every night regardless of actual workload
An Amazon EMR cluster running Presto configured to replace Redshift

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Redshift Serverless scales compute automatically and charges for usage, fitting unpredictable workloads.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Fixed cluster for peak: idle cost.
• Pause nightly: doesn't fit variable weeks.
• EMR Presto: replaces the warehouse.

Key takeaway: unpredictable analytics → Redshift Serverless.

stem: A dataset has one row per (product, month, sales_amount). An analyst wants to reshape it so each row represents one product, with a separate column for each month's sales_amount. Which operation accomplishes this transformation?

choices.text: A GROUP BY clause with no aggregate function
A UNION ALL of the rows
An INNER JOIN of the table with itself
A pivot operation

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A pivot turns row values (months) into columns, one row per product.

Why the other options are wrong:
• GROUP BY without aggregate: no reshaping.
• UNION ALL: stacks rows.
• Self join: not pivoting.

Key takeaway: rows to columns → pivot.

stem: Each file must be checked immediately after upload for header row and row count before the pipeline proceeds, and failures must stop the next stage. Which design fits?

choices.text: A nightly crawler that checks headers
An Athena query run weekly
A full EMR job per file for validation
An S3-triggered validation Lambda

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A lightweight Lambda triggered by the upload performs quick checks and reports success or failure (for example, by moving the file or emitting an event) so downstream stages proceed only on valid files.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Nightly crawler: late, and crawlers don't validate.
• EMR per file: heavy.
• Weekly query: too late.

Key takeaway: light, immediate checks → event-triggered Lambda.

stem: Security must find who deleted a Glue table and from which IP two weeks ago. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS CloudTrail
AWS Glue job bookmarks
Amazon CloudWatch metrics
Amazon Macie

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudTrail records API calls such as glue:DeleteTable, with identity, time, and source IP; event history keeps 90 days of management events.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Metrics: no caller identity.
• Bookmarks: track processed data.
• Macie: sensitive data.

Key takeaway: who did what → CloudTrail.

stem: A Glue Spark job failed. Where are the driver and executor logs, and how can failures be seen by stage?

choices.text: On the Glue console home page only
CloudWatch Logs; the Spark UI shows stages
In CloudTrail data events for the job's S3 reads
In the job's S3 script location

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Glue sends driver and executor logs to CloudWatch Logs (continuous logging can stream them during the run). The Spark UI, enabled with event logs, shows stages and tasks.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Script location: holds code.
• CloudTrail: API calls.
• Console home: summaries only.

Key takeaway: Glue logs → CloudWatch; Spark detail → Spark UI.

stem: The team must be emailed within minutes whenever any Glue job fails or times out. Which setup fits?

choices.text: A daily Athena query over job history
EventBridge job-state rule → SNS email
A CloudTrail trail with S3 delivery
AWS Config rule on Glue jobs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Glue emits job state change events to EventBridge. A rule matching FAILED or TIMEOUT states can publish to an SNS topic with email subscriptions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Daily query: too slow.
• CloudTrail: API calls, not job states.
• Config: configuration compliance.

Key takeaway: job state alerts → EventBridge + SNS.

stem: An AWS Glue Spark job repeatedly fails with out-of-memory errors on the executors when processing a large dataset, though the same job succeeds on smaller datasets. Which change is most likely to resolve this?

choices.text: Add workers or use a larger worker type
Switch the job type from PySpark to a Python shell job
Decrease the job's timeout parameter
Change the job's IAM role to use AdministratorAccess

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Executor out-of-memory errors call for more workers or a larger worker type (such as G.2X) with more memory per executor.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Python shell: less power.
• Shorter timeout: unrelated.
• AdministratorAccess: unrelated.

Key takeaway: Glue OOM → bigger or more workers.

stem: An EMR cluster using EC2 Spot Instances for task nodes experiences intermittent job failures correlated with Spot Instance interruption notices, while the master and core nodes run On-Demand. What is the best practice to reduce failures caused by these interruptions?

choices.text: Store all HDFS data exclusively on the Spot task nodes for faster local access
Disable YARN node health checks
Move the master node to Spot Instances as well, to save additional cost
Spot only on task nodes, with diversified instance fleets

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Keep Spot on task nodes only, which hold no HDFS data. Master and core nodes stay On-Demand so interruptions don't lose data.

Why the other options are wrong:
• HDFS on Spot: data loss.
• Disable health checks: hides failures.
• Spot master: cluster loss.

Key takeaway: EMR Spot → task nodes only.

stem: A data engineer wants to find the count of ERROR-level log entries per 5-minute interval across a Lambda function's CloudWatch log group over the last 24 hours, without exporting the logs anywhere else. Which tool should be used?

choices.text: AWS Trusted Advisor
Amazon Athena, after manually copying the logs into S3 first
The AWS X-Ray service map
Logs Insights: stats count() by bin(5m)

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudWatch Logs Insights can count ERROR entries per 5-minute bin with stats count(*) by bin(5m).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Trusted Advisor: no.
• Copy to S3 for Athena: unnecessary.
• X-Ray map: traces.

Key takeaway: time-bucketed log counts → Logs Insights.

stem: A team has VPC Flow Logs and ALB access logs delivered to an S3 bucket in a consistent partitioned format. They want to run complex, ad hoc SQL joins across both log types to investigate a security incident, without provisioning any servers. Which service is best suited?

choices.text: AWS Trusted Advisor
AWS CloudTrail Insights
Amazon Athena, querying both log sets directly from S3 using SQL
Amazon Inspector

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Athena queries both log sets directly in S3 with SQL, including joins, using tables over the partitioned paths.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Trusted Advisor, CloudTrail Insights, Inspector: not log query tools.

Key takeaway: ad hoc SQL on S3 logs → Athena.

stem: Application logs stream in, and engineers need full-text search and interactive visualizations within seconds of ingestion. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon OpenSearch Service with Dashboards
Amazon Athena over logs delivered to S3
Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL
Amazon Redshift

explanation:
Why this is correct:
OpenSearch indexes logs for near-real-time full-text search and provides dashboards for visualization.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Redshift: analytics, not full-text log search.
• Athena: queries files in S3 after delivery.
• RDS: not designed for log search at scale.

Key takeaway: interactive log search → OpenSearch.

stem: Users report that ad hoc analytical queries in Amazon Redshift are taking much longer than usual to start executing, even though the queries themselves are simple. Reviewing the cluster shows many queries queued concurrently. Which action is most likely to address this?

choices.text: Enable S3 bucket versioning on the underlying data lake
Convert all analytical queries into stored procedures
Add read replicas to the Redshift cluster
Tune WLM queues, such as a queue for ad hoc work

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Slow ad hoc queries during busy periods often come from queueing. Review and adjust WLM queues, concurrency, or enable concurrency scaling.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 versioning: unrelated.
• Stored procedures: no.
• Read replicas: not a Redshift feature.

Key takeaway: query queueing → WLM tuning.

stem: Operations wants a monthly trend of successful versus failed Glue job runs, with an alarm if failures exceed 5 in an hour. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Job-state events as metrics, with an alarm
AWS Config compliance history
S3 server access logs on the script bucket
VPC Flow Logs from the Glue ENIs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Glue job state change events in EventBridge can feed counts into CloudWatch metrics (for example, via a rule and Lambda, or Glue's job observability metrics), which support trends and alarms.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 logs: script access.
• Config: configuration.
• Flow logs: network traffic.

Key takeaway: job outcome trends → events turned into metrics.

stem: A data engineer wants an AWS Glue ETL job's data quality check to automatically fail if more than 2% of rows have a null value in the customer_id column. Which approach should be used?

choices.text: Add a CHECK constraint on the destination Redshift table
Rely on the Glue crawler to detect and automatically reject rows with a null customer_id
A DQDL completeness rule that fails the job
Manually inspect a sample of rows in the Athena console after each job run

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A Glue Data Quality ruleset in DQDL (for example, a completeness threshold) can fail the job when too many values are null.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Redshift CHECK constraints: not enforced.
• Crawler rejects: no.
• Manual inspection: no automation.

Key takeaway: automated quality gates → Glue Data Quality.

stem: A data engineer suspects that a column expected to contain only US state abbreviations actually contains inconsistent values, such as full state names mixed with abbreviations and some typos. Which DataBrew feature would most directly help investigate this before deciding on cleaning rules?

choices.text: Run a DataBrew profile job on the column
Immediately delete the column from the dataset
Increase the DataBrew project's sample size setting without reviewing any output
Export the dataset unmodified to Amazon Redshift

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A DataBrew profile job shows value distributions and unexpected values in the column.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Delete column: loses data.
• Bigger sample without profiling: no insight.
• Export unmodified: no check.

Key takeaway: inspect column values → profiling.

stem: A data engineer wants to profile a 500 GB dataset in AWS Glue DataBrew but needs the sample to proportionally represent each category in a highly imbalanced customer_segment column, rather than just taking the first N rows. Which sampling approach is most appropriate?

choices.text: Stratified sampling to keep category proportions
Sampling only the most recent 24 hours of data regardless of category distribution
Using the entire 500 GB dataset with no sampling on every profiling run
Sequential sampling, taking only the first 500 rows in the file's original order

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Stratified sampling preserves the proportions of groups in the sample, so the profile represents the full dataset.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Last 24 hours only: biased.
• Full dataset every time: slow.
• First 500 rows: biased.

Key takeaway: representative samples → stratified sampling.

stem: A Spark join on customer_id runs one task for 2 hours while the others finish in minutes. One customer has 40% of the rows. What is happening, and what helps?

choices.text: Too many executors; reduce the cluster size
Data skew; salt the hot key or use AQE skew joins
Network timeouts; raise the timeout values
Insufficient partitions for small keys; merge files

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Skew puts a disproportionate share of data in one partition. Salting the hot key or enabling Spark's adaptive query execution skew-join handling spreads the work.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Fewer executors: makes it slower.
• Timeouts: symptom, not cause.
• Merging files: doesn't fix key skew.

Key takeaway: one slow task + hot key = skew.

stem: A Spark job on EMR performs a groupByKey/join on a customer_id field, but a small number of power-user customer_id values account for a disproportionate share of all records, causing a few tasks to run far longer than the rest and stall the entire job. Which technique is most effective at mitigating this data skew?

choices.text: Salt the skewed key to spread its records
Repartition the data into a single partition to guarantee even distribution
Disable Spark's speculative execution entirely
Reduce the number of Spark executors to force more sequential processing

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Salting adds a random suffix to skewed keys, spreading their rows across partitions (with a matching salted join).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Single partition: no parallelism.
• Disable speculation: doesn't fix skew.
• Fewer executors: slower.

Key takeaway: key skew → salting.

stem: A team configures a DataBrew data quality rule checking that the email column matches a valid email pattern, with a threshold requiring at least 95% of rows to pass. If a run shows 92% of rows matching the pattern, what is the outcome?

choices.text: The rule automatically passes, because DataBrew rounds thresholds up to the nearest whole dataset
The ruleset is skipped entirely because the threshold was not met exactly
DataBrew halts all data quality monitoring for the entire AWS account until manually reset
The rule fails, because the passing percentage (92%) is below the configured 95% threshold

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The rule fails because 92% of values passing is below the configured threshold.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Rounds up: no.
• Ruleset skipped: no.
• Halts monitoring: no.

Key takeaway: quality rules compare pass rates to thresholds.

stem: A Lambda function reads from s3://raw/ and writes to s3://curated/. Security requires least privilege and no long-term keys. Which setup fits?

choices.text: An IAM user's access keys in environment variables
A role with only the needed Get/Put permissions
AmazonS3FullAccess on the execution role
Public bucket policies so no IAM is needed

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The execution role provides temporary credentials, and scoping actions and resources to exactly what's needed applies least privilege.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Access keys: long-term credentials.
• Full access: over-privileged.
• Public buckets: exposes data.

Key takeaway: scope role permissions to actions and resources.

stem: A Redshift admin password must rotate every 30 days, and applications must keep working without code changes. Which approach fits?

choices.text: A calendar reminder to change the password manually
Secrets Manager automatic rotation; apps fetch the secret
Parameter Store standard parameters with no rotation
KMS automatic key rotation on the cluster

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Secrets Manager rotates supported database credentials on a schedule and updates the secret, so applications that retrieve the secret at runtime keep working.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Manual change: error-prone.
• Parameter Store: no built-in rotation.
• KMS rotation: rotates encryption keys, not passwords.

Key takeaway: password rotation → Secrets Manager.

stem: An Amazon EC2-hosted ETL job needs to write data to an Amazon S3 bucket but must never traverse the public internet. The security team also requires that the traffic be controlled through a resource-level endpoint policy in addition to IAM permissions. Which change should the data engineer make?

choices.text: Attach an internet gateway to the private subnet
Create a NAT gateway and route S3 traffic through it
An S3 gateway endpoint with a bucket-scoped policy
Add an inbound rule to the EC2 security group allowing traffic to S3's public IP range

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A gateway VPC endpoint for S3, with an endpoint policy, keeps S3 traffic on the AWS network without the internet.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Internet gateway: internet.
• NAT gateway: internet path.
• Inbound SG rule: irrelevant.

Key takeaway: private S3 access → gateway endpoint.

stem: A team is exposing a data ingestion pipeline through Amazon API Gateway, which must invoke a backend AWS Lambda function. What is the correct way to grant API Gateway permission to invoke the Lambda function?

choices.text: Make the Lambda function public by removing all resource policies
Create an IAM user for API Gateway and store its access keys in the Lambda function
Configure a VPC peering connection between API Gateway and Lambda
A resource-based permission for API Gateway on the function

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A resource-based permission on the Lambda function lets API Gateway invoke it.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Make public: insecure.
• IAM user keys: insecure.
• VPC peering: irrelevant.

Key takeaway: service-to-Lambda → resource-based policy.

stem: A team compares PostgreSQL on RDS with PostgreSQL on EC2 for a pipeline database. Which responsibility split is correct?

choices.text: Both: AWS patches everything, including your SQL
EC2: AWS patches the OS; RDS: you patch the engine
Both: you patch the hypervisor and host hardware
RDS: AWS patches OS and engine; EC2: you patch both

explanation:
Why this is correct:
With RDS, AWS manages the OS and database engine patching (in maintenance windows). On EC2, the customer owns the OS and database software. Customers always manage their data, access, and network settings.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS patching EC2's OS: customer responsibility.
• AWS patching everything: data and access remain yours.
• Hypervisor: always AWS.

Key takeaway: managed services move patching to AWS.

stem: A central platform team wants to deploy a standard set of IAM roles and logging resources across 40 AWS member accounts in an organization using AWS CloudFormation StackSets, without manually assuming a role in each account. What must be configured first?

choices.text: An S3 bucket policy granting PutObject to every account ID
StackSets trusted access with service-managed permissions
A Secrets Manager secret replicated to every member account
An AWS Config aggregator in the management account

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Enabling trusted access for CloudFormation StackSets in Organizations allows service-managed StackSets to deploy baselines across member accounts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Bucket policy: unrelated.
• Replicated secret: unrelated.
• Config aggregator: read-only.

Key takeaway: org-wide stack deployment → StackSets trusted access.

stem: Within Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio, which hierarchy correctly describes how access and resources are organized for teams collaborating on data and ML assets?

choices.text: Domains contain domain units, which contain projects
Access is controlled solely through S3 bucket policies with no domain concept
Projects contain domains, and domains contain IAM users directly
A single global namespace shared by all AWS accounts with no further subdivision

explanation:
Why this is correct:
In SageMaker Unified Studio, a domain contains domain units, and domain units contain projects where members collaborate.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 policies only: no.
• Projects contain domains: reversed.
• Single global namespace: no.

Key takeaway: domain → domain units → projects.

stem: A data engineer must grant a group of analysts permission to run Amazon Athena queries only against tables in a specific Glue Data Catalog database, and must not allow them to modify or delete tables. Which approach best follows least privilege?

choices.text: Attach the AdministratorAccess managed policy to the analysts' IAM group
Use the AmazonAthenaFullAccess managed policy for all analysts
Grant the analysts IAM users root account access
A custom read-only policy scoped to the database

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A custom IAM policy allowing only the required Athena actions, workgroup, Glue tables, and S3 locations gives least privilege.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AdministratorAccess: excessive.
• AthenaFullAccess: broad.
• Root access: never.

Key takeaway: least privilege → custom scoped policy.

stem: An app needs a database password that rotates, plus a non-secret batch-size setting that changes occasionally, at the lowest cost. Which split fits?

choices.text: Both in Parameter Store SecureString without rotation
Both in Secrets Manager
Password in Secrets Manager; setting in Parameter Store
Both hardcoded in the application

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Secrets Manager provides rotation for credentials. Parameter Store standard parameters are free and fit plain configuration.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Both in Secrets Manager: pays for non-secret config.
• SecureString without rotation: misses the rotation need.
• Hardcoded: inflexible and insecure.

Key takeaway: secrets with rotation vs. plain config: different stores.

stem: A company wants IAM permissions to automatically apply to any new Amazon S3 bucket that is tagged with project=analytics, without editing the policy each time a new bucket is created. Which authorization approach does this describe?

choices.text: ABAC with resource tags in policy conditions
Discretionary access control using S3 bucket ACLs
Role-based access control using a fixed list of bucket ARNs
Network-based access control using security groups

explanation:
Why this is correct:
ABAC using resource tags applies permissions automatically to any bucket carrying the matching tag.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Bucket ACLs: manual.
• Fixed ARN lists: need updates.
• Security groups: not for S3.

Key takeaway: automatic access by tags → ABAC.

stem: A rapidly growing organization is deciding between a purely role-based access control (RBAC) model, where a new IAM role is created for every job function and resource combination, and an attribute-based access control (ABAC) model using tags for the same access requirements. What is a key operational tradeoff of choosing RBAC over ABAC as the number of teams and resources scales?

choices.text: RBAC automatically inherits permissions from resource tags without configuration
ABAC cannot be implemented in IAM at all
RBAC requires no policy management at all once created
RBAC causes role sprawl; ABAC scales with tags

explanation:
Why this is correct:
RBAC can lead to role and policy sprawl as teams grow, requiring many updates. ABAC scales via tags.

Why the other options are wrong:
• RBAC inherits tags: no.
• ABAC impossible in IAM: false.
• RBAC needs no management: false.

Key takeaway: RBAC sprawl vs. ABAC scale.

stem: A new analyst needs SELECT on two schemas in Redshift and nothing else, and future tables in those schemas should be readable too. Which approach fits?

choices.text: An IAM policy granting redshift:*
A superuser account for the analyst
A role with USAGE, SELECT, and default privileges
The admin user's credentials

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Database privileges are granted with GRANT (USAGE on schema, SELECT on tables) to roles or groups. ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES covers tables created later.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Admin credentials and superuser: over-privileged.
• redshift:*: IAM control-plane actions, not table privileges.

Key takeaway: table-level access in Redshift = SQL GRANTs.

stem: An IAM role has an attached policy that allows glue:GetTable and s3:GetObject on a Lake Formation-governed table, but when the role's user tries to query the table through Amazon Athena, the query fails with an access denied error. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: It lacks the Lake Formation grant on the table
The S3 bucket has been deleted
The IAM policy syntax is invalid JSON
Athena does not support Lake Formation-governed tables

explanation:
Why this is correct:
For Lake Formation-governed tables, the role needs both IAM permissions and Lake Formation grants on the table.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Deleted bucket: different error.
• Invalid JSON: policy wouldn't save.
• Athena unsupported: it's supported.

Key takeaway: governed tables need Lake Formation grants.

stem: A team is configuring encryption for a new Amazon S3 bucket using AWS KMS (SSE-KMS). They must decide who can use the KMS key to decrypt objects. Which statement correctly distinguishes the roles of the KMS key policy and an IAM policy attached to a user in this scenario?

choices.text: Only the KMS key policy matters; IAM policies have no effect on KMS key usage
Both the key policy and the IAM policy must allow it
The IAM policy alone is sufficient; the KMS key policy is ignored for cross-service encryption
S3 bucket policies alone control KMS key usage

explanation:
Why this is correct:
With SSE-KMS, the KMS key policy must allow the principal to use the key, and IAM policies must also permit it where the key policy delegates.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Only key policy: IAM also matters.
• IAM alone: key policy required.
• Bucket policy alone: no.

Key takeaway: KMS access = key policy + IAM.

stem: A company wants to ensure that all requests to its Amazon S3 bucket, whether from applications or users, are rejected unless they use HTTPS, to guarantee encryption in transit. Which solution enforces this requirement?

choices.text: Attach a VPC endpoint policy only, with no bucket policy change
Deny requests where aws:SecureTransport is false
Enable default SSE-S3 encryption on the bucket
Enable S3 Versioning on the bucket

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A bucket policy denying requests where aws:SecureTransport is false forces HTTPS for all requests.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Endpoint policy only: doesn't cover all paths.
• SSE-S3: at rest.
• Versioning: unrelated.

Key takeaway: enforce TLS → SecureTransport deny.

stem: Data scientists query a Redshift table with names and SSNs. They must see masked SSNs, while a compliance role sees full values, from the same table. Which feature fits?

choices.text: KMS encryption of the SSN column with a separate key
Redshift dynamic data masking policies by role
A separate masked copy of the table per team
Row-level security on the table only

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Dynamic data masking applies masking policies at query time based on the user's role, so the same table returns masked or full values.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Masked copy: duplication and sync issues.
• KMS encryption: at-rest protection; authorized queries see plaintext.
• Row-level security: filters rows, not column values.

Key takeaway: role-based column masking → dynamic data masking.

stem: Account A owns an Amazon S3 bucket with objects encrypted using a customer managed AWS KMS key. Account B needs to read those objects using a role in its own account. What must be configured to allow this cross-account decryption?

choices.text: Nothing; KMS keys work across accounts by default
A's key policy must grant B's role kms:Decrypt
Account B must create its own copy of the KMS key
Only the S3 bucket policy needs to be updated; KMS permissions are not required across accounts

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Account B's role needs kms:Decrypt granted in Account A's key policy (plus its own IAM permission and bucket access).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Works by default: no.
• Copy the key: impossible.
• Bucket policy only: KMS also needed.

Key takeaway: cross-account SSE-KMS → key policy grant.

stem: A requirement states that data must be encrypted before leaving the application and that AWS services must only ever store ciphertext. Which approach fits?

choices.text: SSE-KMS on the destination bucket
TLS for data in transit only
SSE-S3 default encryption
Client-side encryption

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Client-side encryption encrypts data in the application before sending it, so services store only ciphertext.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SSE-KMS and SSE-S3: the service encrypts after receiving plaintext.
• TLS: protects transit only.

Key takeaway: encrypt before sending → client-side encryption.

stem: An application that has been successfully decrypting data for months suddenly cannot decrypt newly retrieved older ciphertext, after the customer manually created a new AWS KMS customer managed key and re-pointed an existing alias to it. What most likely explains the behavior?

choices.text: This indicates a Secrets Manager rotation failure, unrelated to KMS
KMS automatically re-encrypts all previously encrypted objects when an alias is updated
Old data still needs the old key to decrypt
KMS deleted the old key material immediately, which is expected behavior for all rotations

explanation:
Why this is correct:
If an alias was re-pointed to a new key, new data is encrypted with the new key. Decrypt failures suggest the app lacks permission on the new key (or old data still needs the old key).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Secrets rotation: unrelated.
• KMS re-encrypts objects: no.
• Old key material deleted: no.

Key takeaway: alias changes switch the key used.

stem: A company must both discover unclassified sensitive data such as PII scattered across S3 buckets and also mask sensitive columns before analysts query a Redshift table. Which pairing of services correctly addresses each need respectively?

choices.text: AWS CloudTrail for discovering PII, and IAM policies for masking query results
Amazon GuardDuty for discovering PII, and Amazon Macie for masking query results
Macie to find PII; Redshift dynamic masking
AWS Config for discovering PII, and AWS KMS for masking query results

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Macie discovers PII in S3, and Redshift dynamic data masking hides sensitive values from query results by role.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudTrail discovery: no.
• GuardDuty discovery: no.
• Config discovery: no.

Key takeaway: discover → Macie; mask → dynamic masking.

stem: A global company operates workloads in two AWS Regions and needs both regions to be able to decrypt the same encrypted data using AWS KMS, with the ability to fail over encryption operations to the second Region during a Regional disruption, while keeping a single logical key identity. Which KMS feature should be used?

choices.text: KMS multi-Region keys in each Region
AWS managed keys (aws/s3)
A single-Region customer managed key shared through IAM cross-account policies
Enabling automatic annual key rotation

explanation:
Why this is correct:
KMS multi-Region keys share key material across Regions, so each Region can decrypt the other's data.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS managed keys: Regional.
• Single-Region key via IAM: can't decrypt elsewhere.
• Rotation: unrelated.

Key takeaway: cross-Region decryption → multi-Region keys.

stem: A security team wants to run SQL-based queries across CloudTrail events aggregated from multiple AWS accounts and Regions, retained for up to several years, without having to first load data into S3 and set up Athena tables manually. Which service best fits this requirement?

choices.text: AWS CloudTrail Lake
Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights
Amazon OpenSearch Service
AWS Config aggregator

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudTrail Lake aggregates events across accounts and Regions into an event data store you query with SQL.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Logs Insights: not SQL across aggregated trails in this way.
• OpenSearch: requires ingestion.
• Config aggregator: configuration.

Key takeaway: SQL on CloudTrail events → CloudTrail Lake.

stem: An organization already delivers its CloudTrail logs to a centralized Amazon S3 bucket and wants to run ad hoc SQL queries against historical logs stored as JSON/gzip files without deploying additional infrastructure. Which service is the most direct fit?

choices.text: Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics
AWS Glue DataBrew
Amazon Redshift Spectrum with a mandatory ETL pipeline
Amazon Athena with a table defined over the CloudTrail S3 log location

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Athena can query CloudTrail logs already in S3 by defining a table (with partition projection), no pipeline needed.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Kinesis Analytics: streams.
• DataBrew: prep.
• Spectrum with ETL: unnecessary.

Key takeaway: CloudTrail in S3 → Athena.

stem: A team must decide between using Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights and Amazon Athena to analyze several terabytes of historical application log data that is already archived in Amazon S3 in Parquet format for infrequent, ad hoc investigations. What is a key tradeoff to consider?

choices.text: Athena cannot query Parquet files under any circumstances
Logs Insights queries log groups; Athena queries S3 data
CloudWatch Logs Insights natively queries data stored in S3 in Parquet format with no additional configuration, making it strictly better for this use case
Both services are functionally identical for this scenario with no meaningful differences

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Logs Insights queries logs stored in CloudWatch Logs. Athena queries data in S3, such as Parquet logs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Athena can't query Parquet: it can.
• Logs Insights queries S3: no.
• Identical: no.

Key takeaway: where the data lives decides the tool.

stem: A security engineer configured an AWS CloudTrail trail expecting it to capture PutObject and DeleteObject events for a sensitive S3 bucket, but the trail's event history only shows CreateBucket and PutBucketPolicy events for that bucket. What most likely explains the gap?

choices.text: CloudTrail cannot log any S3 events under any configuration
The trail logs management events, not data events
The S3 bucket has server-side encryption disabled
The IAM role used by the application lacks a trust policy

explanation:
Why this is correct:
PutObject and DeleteObject are data events. A trail logging only management events won't capture them.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudTrail can't log S3: it can.
• Encryption: unrelated.
• Trust policy: unrelated.

Key takeaway: object operations need data events.

stem: A compliance team wants to be notified in near real time whenever a CloudTrail event shows that an IAM policy was attached granting administrator-level permissions to any user. Which integration should be built?

choices.text: Manually review the CloudTrail console once a day
An EventBridge rule on the API call, notifying via SNS
Create an AWS Config conformance pack with no further action
Enable S3 default encryption on the CloudTrail log bucket

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An EventBridge rule matching the specific CloudTrail event triggers a notification (for example, SNS) in near real time.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Daily review: slow.
• Conformance pack alone: no notification.
• Log bucket encryption: unrelated.

Key takeaway: near-real-time alerts on API calls → EventBridge.

stem: Logs from many sources must be centralized for interactive search, dashboards, and anomaly alerts within seconds. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Glue streaming ETL
Amazon OpenSearch Service
Amazon Redshift
Amazon Athena

explanation:
Why this is correct:
OpenSearch provides indexing, search, dashboards, and alerting and anomaly detection plugins for near-real-time log analytics.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Redshift: batch-oriented analytics.
• Athena: queries files after delivery.
• Glue: ETL.

Key takeaway: log analytics platform → OpenSearch.

stem: A producer Redshift workgroup must give a consumer team in another account live read access to three schemas, without copying data or building ETL. Which feature fits?

choices.text: A DMS task replicating the tables
UNLOAD to S3 and COPY into the consumer
Redshift data sharing (cross-account)
A nightly snapshot restored in the consumer account

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Data sharing grants live, read-only access to databases, schemas, or tables across clusters or workgroups, including across accounts, without moving data.

Why the other options are wrong:
• UNLOAD/COPY: copies data and adds latency.
• Snapshot restore: a copy and stale.
• DMS: replication and cost.

Key takeaway: share live data without copies → data sharing.

stem: A governance team wants to automatically discover columns containing PII across many S3-based data lake tables and then enforce that only authorized roles can query those specific columns through the data lake's catalog. Which combination of services and workflow achieves this?

choices.text: Use AWS Config alone to both discover and restrict access to PII columns
Use Macie findings to drive Lake Formation access
Rely solely on S3 bucket policies to restrict access to PII, with no cataloging involved
Use CloudTrail Insights to discover PII patterns in API calls

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Macie finds PII in S3, and its findings can drive restrictions such as Lake Formation tags or permissions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Config alone: no content discovery.
• Bucket policies alone: no discovery.
• CloudTrail Insights: API anomalies.

Key takeaway: discover PII, then restrict.

stem: After a pipeline broke, the team needs to see when a bucket policy and a Glue connection were changed, and what the previous settings were. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Config configuration history
Amazon CloudWatch metrics
Amazon Macie bucket inventory
AWS Trusted Advisor

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Config records resource configurations over time and shows what changed and when, alongside related CloudTrail events.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Metrics: performance, not configuration.
• Macie: sensitive data.
• Trusted Advisor: best-practice checks.

Key takeaway: what was the configuration before? → Config.

stem: A multinational company must ensure that customer data belonging to European Union residents is never stored or processed outside EU AWS Regions, to comply with data sovereignty requirements. Which combination of controls best enforces this at the account/organization level?

choices.text: Enable CloudTrail logging in all Regions with no preventive controls
SCPs denying actions outside approved EU Regions
Use Amazon Macie to physically move data between Regions automatically
Rely only on application-level checks in each microservice

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SCPs denying actions outside approved EU Regions prevent data from being stored elsewhere.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudTrail only: detective.
• Macie moves data: no.
• App checks only: bypassable.

Key takeaway: residency → SCP Region restrictions.

stem: In the Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio governance model, how do project members typically gain governed access to shared data assets like tables and datasets that have been published for reuse across teams?

choices.text: There is no concept of shared or catalog assets in SageMaker Unified Studio
Every project member is granted account-wide IAM administrator access
Through the project's catalog subscriptions
Data assets are copied unencrypted to each member's local machine

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Project members access published data assets through their project's subscriptions and project roles, not personal broad permissions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• No shared assets: false.
• Account-wide admin: no.
• Unencrypted local copies: no.

Key takeaway: access via project subscriptions.

stem: Two business units in the same company, each running its own AWS account, need Business Unit B to run analytical queries against a curated subset of Business Unit A's data lake tables, while Business Unit A retains ownership and control over the underlying data and its permissions. Which pattern best fits this cross-account data governance requirement?

choices.text: A shares tables with B's account via Lake Formation
Business Unit B is given the root credentials of Business Unit A's account
Both accounts are merged into a single AWS account to simplify governance
Business Unit A exports full table dumps to Business Unit B's S3 bucket weekly

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Business Unit A registers its data in Lake Formation and grants B's account cross-account access to specific tables.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Root credentials: never.
• Merge accounts: disruptive.
• Full dumps: duplication.

Key takeaway: cross-account data sharing → Lake Formation grants.

stem: A company enabled an AWS Config managed rule to flag any S3 bucket that does not have default encryption enabled, but a newly created noncompliant bucket does not appear as noncompliant in the AWS Config dashboard even after several hours. What is a likely cause the engineer should investigate first?

choices.text: The bucket must be manually deleted and recreated for Config to notice it
AWS Config evaluates resources only once per year regardless of changes
Config isn't recording S3 in that Region
S3 buckets cannot be evaluated by AWS Config managed rules

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Config can't evaluate resources it isn't recording. Enable the recorder for S3 bucket resources.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Recreate bucket: no.
• Yearly evaluation: false.
• S3 unsupported: supported.

Key takeaway: no evaluations → check the recorder.

stem: Clickstream JSON events must land in S3 as Parquet within a few minutes for Athena queries, with no custom consumer code to maintain. Which solution fits BEST?

choices.text: Kinesis Data Streams with a custom KCL application that converts to Parquet.
Amazon SQS with Lambda writing one file per event.
An hourly Glue job that reads JSON and writes CSV.
Data Firehose with Parquet record format conversion.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Firehose with record format conversion buffers JSON events, converts them to Parquet using a Glue schema, and delivers to S3 within minutes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Custom KCL app: more code.
• One file per event: tiny files.
• Hourly Glue to CSV: slow and wrong format.

Key takeaway: stream to Parquet in S3 → Firehose conversion.

stem: A Kinesis data stream with 20 shards shows WriteProvisionedThroughputExceeded errors on one shard while the others are nearly idle. The partition key is the event type, and 90% of events are 'page_view'. What is the BEST fix?

choices.text: Use a higher-cardinality partition key.
Switch the producer to synchronous PutRecord calls.
Double the number of shards.
Increase the data retention period.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Errors on one shard mean a hot partition key. A higher-cardinality key, such as session ID, spreads writes across shards.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Synchronous calls: slower.
• More shards: the hot key still hits one shard.
• Retention: unrelated.

Key takeaway: one hot shard → better partition key.

stem: A nightly Glue job reprocesses all files in an S3 prefix, even though only new files arrive each day. Runtime and cost keep growing. What should the data engineer enable?

choices.text: Glue job bookmarks so only unprocessed data is read.
A Glue crawler before every run.
S3 Versioning on the input bucket.
More DPUs for the job.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Glue job bookmarks track processed files, so each run reads only new data.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Crawler: cataloging.
• Versioning: unrelated.
• More DPUs: still reprocesses.

Key takeaway: incremental processing → bookmarks.

stem: Athena queries on a streaming data lake are slow. The table contains millions of files averaging 20 KB. What is the MOST effective improvement?

choices.text: Add more columns to each file.
Switch the files to uncompressed JSON.
Increase Athena's query timeout.
Compact the small files into larger files (for example, 128 MB-1 GB Parquet) and increase upstream buffering.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Millions of tiny files add per-file overhead. Compacting into larger files (for example, 128 MB or more) speeds Athena queries.

Why the other options are wrong:
• More columns: no.
• Uncompressed JSON: slower.
• Longer timeout: no.

Key takeaway: small files → compaction.

stem: A team already has 150 Apache Airflow DAGs orchestrating Glue, EMR, and Redshift tasks on self-managed servers. It wants a managed service with minimal rewrite. Which option fits BEST?

choices.text: Amazon EventBridge Scheduler with Lambda.
AWS Glue workflows only.
Amazon Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow (MWAA).
Rewrite all workflows in AWS Step Functions.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
MWAA runs existing Airflow DAGs as a managed service with minimal changes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Scheduler with Lambda: rewrite.
• Glue workflows only: rewrite.
• Step Functions: rewrite 150 workflows.

Key takeaway: existing Airflow → MWAA.

stem: An on-premises MySQL database must feed a data lake in S3 with inserts, updates, and deletes within minutes, without impacting the source with repeated full exports. Which solution fits BEST?

choices.text: A Glue crawler pointed at the MySQL database.
Amazon AppFlow from MySQL.
Nightly mysqldump files uploaded to S3.
AWS DMS full load plus ongoing CDC.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
DMS with a full load plus ongoing CDC continuously replicates inserts, updates, and deletes into S3.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Crawler: metadata.
• AppFlow: SaaS sources.
• Nightly dumps: no CDC.

Key takeaway: continuous DB changes → DMS CDC.

stem: Two large Redshift tables, orders and order_items, are frequently joined on order_id. Queries show heavy data redistribution across nodes. Which change reduces this?

choices.text: Add more sort keys.
Use KEY distribution on order_id for both tables so matching rows are colocated.
Set DISTSTYLE ALL on both large tables.
Use EVEN distribution on both tables.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
KEY distribution on order_id for both tables co-locates matching rows, avoiding redistribution during joins.

Why the other options are wrong:
• More sort keys: no collocation.
• ALL on large tables: huge storage.
• EVEN: redistribution.

Key takeaway: frequent large joins → shared distribution key.

stem: A data lake must support deleting a specific customer's records within 30 days of a request (GDPR), with ACID guarantees and time travel for audits. Which table format fits BEST?

choices.text: JSON files with S3 Object Lock.
Apache Iceberg tables queried with Athena or Glue.
Plain Parquet files partitioned by date.
CSV files with a manifest.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Apache Iceberg tables support row-level deletes, so specific customers' records can be removed efficiently.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Object Lock: prevents deletion.
• Plain Parquet: rewrite files manually.
• CSV with manifest: no row-level deletes.

Key takeaway: row-level deletes in a data lake → Iceberg.

stem: A crawler over s3://logs/app/ creates hundreds of separate tables instead of one table, because some files have slightly different column sets. What should the engineer configure?

choices.text: Configure the crawler to combine compatible schemas into a single table per S3 path (table grouping options).
Delete all files with extra columns.
Run the crawler more frequently.
Use a different Region.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Configuring the crawler to combine compatible schemas (grouping behavior) creates a single table despite minor column differences.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Delete files: data loss.
• Run more often: same result.
• Different Region: no.

Key takeaway: one table from varied files → crawler grouping settings.

stem: A Redshift warehouse holds 2 years of hot data, but analysts occasionally need 8 years of history that is stored in S3 as Parquet. Loading all history into Redshift is too expensive. What should the team use?

choices.text: Redshift Spectrum external tables.
Export Redshift data to CSV for Excel.
COPY all history into Redshift every quarter.
Move the entire warehouse to DynamoDB.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Redshift Spectrum external tables query historical data in S3 alongside hot data in Redshift, without loading it.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CSV for Excel: no.
• COPY all history: costly.
• DynamoDB: wrong store.

Key takeaway: hot in Redshift, cold in S3 → Spectrum.

stem: Producers on Amazon MSK occasionally change event schemas and break downstream consumers. The team wants to block incompatible schema changes at produce time. Which solution fits BEST?

choices.text: Increase topic retention.
Use a single partition per topic.
Document schemas in a wiki.
Use the AWS Glue Schema Registry with a compatibility mode such as BACKWARD and serializers that validate schemas.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The Glue Schema Registry enforces compatibility modes, so incompatible schema changes are rejected before breaking consumers.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Retention: unrelated.
• Single partition: throughput.
• Wiki: not enforcement.

Key takeaway: schema evolution control → Schema Registry.

stem: Several teams share Athena, and one team's ad hoc queries have scanned tens of terabytes, causing cost overruns. How can the data platform team limit this?

choices.text: Use Athena workgroups with per-query data usage limits and separate query result locations.
Enable S3 Requester Pays.
Delete the team's IAM users.
Convert all data to JSON.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Athena workgroups with per-query data usage limits (and workgroup limits) cap how much a team's queries can scan.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Requester Pays: S3 billing.
• Delete users: drastic.
• JSON: more scanning.

Key takeaway: control Athena spend → workgroup limits.

stem: A pipeline must stop before loading data into the warehouse if more than 1% of rows have null customer_id or if order totals are negative. Which approach fits BEST?

choices.text: Rely on Redshift to reject nulls automatically.
Glue Data Quality rules that fail the job.
Increase the job's DPUs.
Check the data manually each morning.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Glue Data Quality rules in DQDL inside the job can fail the pipeline when null rates exceed 1%, before loading.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Redshift rejects nulls: not automatically for this rule.
• More DPUs: unrelated.
• Manual checks: no automation.

Key takeaway: gate loads on data quality → Glue Data Quality.

stem: A dashboard runs the same complex aggregation over large Redshift tables every few minutes, and queries take 40 seconds. Underlying data changes hourly. What is the MOST effective improvement?

choices.text: Create a materialized view with auto refresh and point the dashboard to it.
Increase the dashboard refresh rate.
Use DISTSTYLE ALL on the fact table.
Disable result caching.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A materialized view with auto refresh precomputes the aggregation, so the dashboard reads results quickly.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Faster refresh: more load.
• DISTSTYLE ALL on fact table: costly.
• Disable result caching: worse.

Key takeaway: repeated heavy aggregations → materialized views.

stem: A Spark join on EMR fails with out-of-memory errors on a few executors while most executors finish quickly. One join key value accounts for 30% of the rows. Which technique addresses this?

choices.text: Increase the number of output files.
Switch the input format to CSV.
Salt the skewed key (or use adaptive query execution skew-join handling), or broadcast the small side of the join.
Add more executors of the same size.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A few executors failing means data skew. Salt the skewed key or enable adaptive query execution skew-join handling.

Why the other options are wrong:
• More output files: no.
• CSV: no.
• More same-size executors: skewed partition still too big.

Key takeaway: skewed joins → salting or AQE.

stem: Analysts in different business units must see only rows for their region and must never see columns tagged as PII, across hundreds of tables. The platform team wants to manage this by classification rather than per table. Which approach fits BEST?

choices.text: Separate copies of every table per region.
IAM policies listing column names.
LF-Tags with row-level data filters.
S3 bucket policies per prefix.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Lake Formation LF-Tags with data filters give row-level (region) and column-level restrictions by business unit.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Separate table copies: duplication.
• IAM column lists: not supported for data.
• Bucket policies per prefix: no column control.

Key takeaway: row + column security in the lake → LF-Tags and data filters.

stem: Customer support staff query a Redshift table that contains credit card numbers. They should see only the last four digits, while the fraud team sees full values, without maintaining separate tables. Which feature fits BEST?

choices.text: Redshift dynamic data masking policies attached to roles.
Column-level encryption with a shared key given to everyone.
Redshift concurrency scaling.
A nightly job creating a masked copy of the table.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Redshift dynamic data masking policies attached to roles show masked card numbers to support staff and full values to authorized roles.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Shared decryption key: no protection.
• Concurrency scaling: performance.
• Nightly masked copy: stale and duplicated.

Key takeaway: role-based masking → dynamic data masking.

stem: A central Redshift cluster owns curated data. Three business units in other AWS accounts need live, read-only access with their own compute, without copying data. Which approach fits BEST?

choices.text: Share the admin password of the producer cluster.
Use DMS to replicate tables continuously.
Cross-account Redshift data sharing.
Unload to S3 and COPY into each account nightly.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Redshift data sharing gives other accounts' clusters live, read-only access to curated data without copying.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Share admin password: insecure.
• DMS replication: copying.
• Nightly UNLOAD/COPY: stale.

Key takeaway: live cross-account sharing → Redshift data sharing.

stem: Security requires that Glue ETL jobs encrypt data written to S3, CloudWatch logs, and job bookmarks with customer managed KMS keys. Which feature enforces this for the jobs?

choices.text: Enabling SSL on the Glue connection.
An IAM policy denying Glue.
Default S3 bucket encryption only.
A Glue security configuration specifying KMS keys for S3, CloudWatch Logs, and bookmark encryption, attached to the jobs.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A Glue security configuration specifies KMS keys for S3 output, CloudWatch Logs, and job bookmarks, applied to jobs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SSL on connections: in transit only.
• Deny Glue: blocks work.
• Default S3 encryption only: doesn't cover logs or bookmarks.

Key takeaway: encrypt all Glue outputs → security configuration.

stem: An application must ingest click events in real time, keep them for seven days, and let several consumers read the same events independently. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon SQS standard queue
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams
AWS Snowball Edge device
Amazon SNS standard topic

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Kinesis Data Streams retains records and supports multiple independent consumers.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon SQS standard queue: SQS deletes messages once consumed by one consumer.
• AWS Snowball Edge device: Snowball is offline transfer.
• Amazon SNS standard topic: SNS does not retain messages.

Key takeaway: Replayable multi-consumer streams → Kinesis Data Streams.

stem: IoT events must be delivered to S3 in near real time, batched, compressed, and converted to Parquet with no custom code. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Glue batch jobs running once per day
Amazon Data Firehose
Amazon EMR cluster running Spark Streaming
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams with custom consumers

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Firehose buffers, compresses, and converts streaming data to Parquet before writing to S3.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Glue batch jobs running once per day: Daily batches are not near real time.
• Amazon EMR cluster running Spark Streaming: EMR requires managing clusters and code.
• Amazon Kinesis Data Streams with custom…: Custom consumers require code.

Key takeaway: Codeless stream delivery to S3 → Data Firehose.

stem: A company must continuously replicate changes from an on-premises Oracle database into S3 for analytics. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Snowball Edge shipped every week
AWS DMS with full load and change data capture
Amazon AppFlow flows from SaaS sources
AWS DataSync scheduled file transfer tasks from the database host

explanation:
Why this is correct:
DMS supports full load plus ongoing CDC from databases to targets such as S3.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Snowball Edge shipped every week: Weekly shipments are not continuous.
• Amazon AppFlow flows from SaaS sources: AppFlow targets SaaS applications.
• AWS DataSync scheduled file transfer tasks…: DataSync moves files, not database changes.

Key takeaway: Database CDC into S3 → DMS.

stem: A company wants to ingest data from Salesforce and ServiceNow into S3 on a schedule without writing code. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Transfer Family
Amazon AppFlow
AWS DataSync
Amazon Kinesis Video Streams

explanation:
Why this is correct:
AppFlow transfers data between SaaS applications and AWS services without code.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Transfer Family: Transfer Family provides SFTP/FTPS endpoints.
• AWS DataSync: DataSync moves file and object storage data.
• Amazon Kinesis Video Streams: Kinesis Video Streams handles video.

Key takeaway: SaaS data ingestion → AppFlow.

stem: Partners must upload files to the company using SFTP, and the files must land directly in S3. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon AppFlow
Amazon MQ
AWS DMS
AWS Transfer Family

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Transfer Family provides managed SFTP endpoints backed by S3.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon AppFlow: AppFlow connects SaaS apps.
• Amazon MQ: Amazon MQ is a message broker.
• AWS DMS: DMS migrates databases.

Key takeaway: Managed SFTP into S3 → Transfer Family.

stem: A company already uses Apache Kafka clients and wants a managed Kafka service on AWS. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon SNS
Amazon MSK
Amazon SQS
AWS Batch

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Amazon MSK runs managed Apache Kafka compatible with existing clients.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon SNS: SNS uses a different API.
• Amazon SQS: SQS uses a different API.
• AWS Batch: Batch runs compute jobs.

Key takeaway: Managed Kafka → Amazon MSK.
