stem: Streaming data must be loaded into Amazon Redshift with low latency for near-real-time dashboards. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Daily COPY commands from a CSV export on S3
Redshift streaming ingestion from Kinesis Data Streams or MSK
Manual INSERT statements run by analysts at the start of each hour
Exporting data to spreadsheets and uploading them

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Streaming ingestion reads directly from Kinesis or MSK into materialized views with low latency.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Daily COPY commands from a CSV export on S3: Daily COPY is not near real time.
• Manual INSERT statements run by analysts at…: Manual inserts are slow and error-prone.
• Exporting data to spreadsheets and uploading…: Spreadsheets are not an ingestion path.

Key takeaway: Low-latency loads into Redshift → streaming ingestion.

stem: Kinesis Data Streams consumers fall behind, and records approach the retention limit. Which TWO actions help? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Decrease retention to one hour
Remove partition keys from records
Reduce the number of consumers to zero
Use enhanced fan-out for heavy consumers
Increase shard count or use on-demand mode

explanation:
Why this is correct:
More shards increase parallelism, and enhanced fan-out gives each consumer dedicated throughput.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Decrease retention to one hour: Shorter retention loses data sooner.
• Remove partition keys from records: Partition keys are required.
• Reduce the number of consumers to zero: No consumers means no processing.

Key takeaway: Scale streams with shards and enhanced fan-out.

stem: A daily Glue ETL job reprocesses all files in an S3 prefix even though only new files arrive each day. Which feature fixes this?

choices.text: Glue job bookmarks
Glue Schema Registry
Glue crawlers only
Glue Data Catalog versions

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Job bookmarks track processed data so jobs process only new files.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Glue Schema Registry: Schema Registry validates streaming schemas.
• Glue crawlers only: Crawlers update the catalog.
• Glue Data Catalog versions: Catalog versions track schema changes.

Key takeaway: Incremental Glue processing → job bookmarks.

stem: A Spark job on EMR is slow because the input consists of millions of tiny files in S3. Which improvement helps most?

choices.text: Convert the files to uncompressed CSV to simplify parsing
Increase the number of files by splitting each existing file into smaller pieces
Add more master nodes to the EMR cluster configuration
Compact small files into larger files, for example 128 MB to 1 GB Parquet

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Compaction reduces per-file overhead and improves read performance.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Convert the files to uncompressed CSV to…: Uncompressed CSV is slower to read.
• Increase the number of files by splitting…: More files worsen overhead.
• Add more master nodes to the EMR cluster…: Master nodes do not fix small-file overhead.

Key takeaway: Fix the small-file problem with compaction.

stem: A team wants serverless Spark ETL with automatic scaling and no cluster management. Which TWO options fit? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Amazon ElastiCache clusters
AWS Glue Spark jobs
Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL
A single EC2 instance with Spark
Amazon EMR Serverless

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Glue and EMR Serverless run Spark without cluster management.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon ElastiCache clusters: ElastiCache is a cache.
• Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL: RDS is a database.
• A single EC2 instance with Spark: Self-managed EC2 requires management and does not scale automatically.

Key takeaway: Serverless Spark → Glue or EMR Serverless.

stem: A transformation must convert CSV to Parquet, partition by date, and register the table for Athena. Which approach needs the least custom infrastructure?

choices.text: Manually converting files in a spreadsheet and uploading them
A Lambda function that loads all data into memory at once
A Glue ETL job writing partitioned Parquet and updating the Data Catalog
A custom Java application on an EC2 instance that converts the files one at a time

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Glue ETL can write partitioned Parquet and update the catalog so Athena can query it.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Manually converting files in a spreadsheet…: Manual work does not scale.
• A Lambda function that loads all data into…: Lambda memory and time limits prevent large loads.
• A custom Java application on an EC2 instance…: Custom EC2 apps require management.

Key takeaway: Convert and catalog data with Glue ETL.

stem: Small JSON files arrive in S3 throughout the day, each needing light validation and enrichment within seconds. Which option fits?

choices.text: A weekly Glue job with bookmarks
A manual review by the data team
S3 event notifications invoking a Lambda function
A nightly EMR cluster that reads all of the day's files

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Event-driven Lambda processes each small file shortly after arrival.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A weekly Glue job with bookmarks: Weekly jobs are too slow.
• A manual review by the data team: Manual review does not scale.
• A nightly EMR cluster that reads all of the…: Nightly processing is too slow.

Key takeaway: Per-file, low-latency processing → S3 events plus Lambda.

stem: A Spark job suffers from data skew, with one partition holding most rows for a popular key. Which technique helps?

choices.text: Removing all partitioning from the output files
Converting the data to CSV before processing
Reducing the number of Spark executors in the cluster
Salting the skewed key to spread records across partitions

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Salting adds randomness to hot keys so work spreads across partitions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Removing all partitioning from the output files: Output partitioning does not fix processing skew.
• Converting the data to CSV before processing: CSV does not fix skew.
• Reducing the number of Spark executors in…: Fewer executors worsen performance.

Key takeaway: Fix key skew with salting.

stem: An analyst needs to rank each customer's orders by date within the customer. Which SQL feature fits?

choices.text: A window function with PARTITION BY customer ORDER BY date
A CROSS JOIN between the orders and customers tables
A GROUP BY customer with MAX(date) only
A DISTINCT on customer and order columns

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Window functions compute rankings within partitions while keeping individual rows.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A CROSS JOIN between the orders and…: Cross joins multiply rows.
• A GROUP BY customer with MAX(date) only: GROUP BY collapses rows.
• A DISTINCT on customer and order columns: DISTINCT removes duplicates.

Key takeaway: Per-group rankings → window functions.

stem: A team wants to create a new optimized table in S3 from an Athena query result, stored as partitioned Parquet. Which feature fits?

choices.text: An Athena SELECT query saved as CSV
CREATE TABLE AS SELECT (CTAS) in Athena
A Glue crawler on the query result bucket
An S3 Select query on the source files

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CTAS writes query results as a new table in the chosen format and partitioning.

Why the other options are wrong:
• An Athena SELECT query saved as CSV: CSV results are not optimized tables.
• A Glue crawler on the query result bucket: Crawlers catalog data, not transform it.
• An S3 Select query on the source files: S3 Select filters single objects.

Key takeaway: Create optimized tables from queries with CTAS.

stem: A pipeline has several dependent steps: ingest, transform with Glue, load into Redshift, then notify. It needs retries and visual monitoring with minimal infrastructure. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Step Functions
Amazon SQS standard queues only
Amazon CloudFront distributions
A cron job on an EC2 instance

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Step Functions orchestrates serverless steps with retries and visual monitoring.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon SQS standard queues only: Queues alone do not orchestrate.
• Amazon CloudFront distributions: CloudFront is a CDN.
• A cron job on an EC2 instance: Cron on EC2 lacks orchestration features.

Key takeaway: Orchestrate pipelines with Step Functions.

stem: A data team already writes DAGs in Apache Airflow and wants a managed environment on AWS. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon EventBridge Scheduler schedules only
AWS Batch compute environments
AWS Glue DataBrew recipe jobs
Amazon Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow

explanation:
Why this is correct:
MWAA runs managed Airflow environments for existing DAGs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon EventBridge Scheduler schedules only: Scheduler triggers tasks but does not run DAGs.
• AWS Batch compute environments: Batch runs compute jobs.
• AWS Glue DataBrew recipe jobs: DataBrew prepares data visually.

Key takeaway: Managed Airflow → MWAA.

stem: A Glue job must start automatically when a file lands in S3. Which approach fits?

choices.text: A data engineer watching the bucket and starting the job manually
A Glue job scheduled every minute to check for new files
An EventBridge rule on the S3 event starting the Glue job or workflow
An S3 lifecycle rule that runs the Glue job after upload

explanation:
Why this is correct:
EventBridge can react to S3 events and start Glue jobs or workflows.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A data engineer watching the bucket and…: Manual starts are unreliable.
• A Glue job scheduled every minute to check…: Frequent polling wastes resources.
• An S3 lifecycle rule that runs the Glue job…: Lifecycle rules cannot run jobs.

Key takeaway: Event-driven pipeline triggers via EventBridge.

stem: Several Glue crawlers and jobs must run in a dependency order with a single view of status. Which Glue feature fits?

choices.text: Glue interactive sessions
Glue workflows with triggers
Glue Schema Registry
Glue DataBrew projects

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Glue workflows chain crawlers and jobs with triggers and show overall status.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Glue interactive sessions: Interactive sessions support development.
• Glue Schema Registry: Schema Registry manages schemas.
• Glue DataBrew projects: DataBrew is for visual data prep.

Key takeaway: Chain Glue components with workflows.

stem: A pipeline step occasionally fails because a downstream API is briefly unavailable. Which TWO features help in Step Functions? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Removing the failing step from the workflow
Disabling logging to speed up the workflow
Running all steps in parallel to avoid ordering
Catch blocks routing failures to a fallback path
Retry with exponential backoff on the task

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Retries handle transient failures, and Catch routes persistent failures to fallback handling.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Removing the failing step from the workflow: Removing steps breaks the pipeline.
• Disabling logging to speed up the workflow: Logging does not affect failures.
• Running all steps in parallel to avoid ordering: Parallelism breaks dependencies.

Key takeaway: Handle failures with Retry and Catch.

stem: A data engineer must reuse a transformation function across several Lambda-based pipelines. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Package the shared code as a Lambda layer
Copy the function into every Lambda by hand
Rewrite the function differently in each pipeline
Store the function in environment variables

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Layers share code across functions and keep it consistent.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Copy the function into every Lambda by hand: Copies drift.
• Rewrite the function differently in each…: Rewriting leads to inconsistencies.
• Store the function in environment variables: Environment variables are not code storage.

Key takeaway: Share pipeline code with layers.

stem: A team wants data pipeline infrastructure (Glue jobs, crawlers, IAM roles, buckets) defined as code and deployed consistently across environments. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Screenshots of production settings used to recreate them
Console configuration copied manually between environments
AWS CDK or CloudFormation deployed through a CI/CD pipeline
A shared text file listing the settings of each resource

explanation:
Why this is correct:
IaC deployed through CI/CD produces consistent, reviewable environments.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Screenshots of production settings used to…: Screenshots are not deployable.
• Console configuration copied manually…: Manual copying drifts.
• A shared text file listing the settings of…: Text files are not deployable.

Key takeaway: Manage data infrastructure as code.

stem: A SQL query in Redshift scans the entire table although it filters on a date column. Which table design change helps?

choices.text: Use DISTSTYLE ALL for the large table
Define a sort key on the date column
Remove compression from all columns
Add more columns to the table

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Sort keys let Redshift skip blocks outside the filtered range.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Use DISTSTYLE ALL for the large table: DISTSTYLE ALL copies the table to every node and suits small tables.
• Remove compression from all columns: Removing compression increases I/O.
• Add more columns to the table: More columns do not reduce scanning.

Key takeaway: Speed range filters with sort keys.

stem: Two large Redshift tables are frequently joined on customer_id, causing heavy data redistribution. Which change helps?

choices.text: Use ALL distribution on both large tables
Use EVEN distribution on both tables
Remove the join and query each table separately
Use KEY distribution on customer_id for both tables

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Distributing both tables on the join key co-locates matching rows, reducing redistribution.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Use ALL distribution on both large tables: ALL is costly for large tables.
• Use EVEN distribution on both tables: EVEN spreads rows randomly and requires redistribution.
• Remove the join and query each table separately: Removing the join changes results.

Key takeaway: Co-locate joins with KEY distribution.

stem: A company needs a Spark transformation to run in response to streaming data with sub-minute latency and managed infrastructure. Which option fits?

choices.text: A Redshift COPY command from S3 every night
An Athena query run manually every hour
Glue streaming ETL or Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink
A daily Glue batch job with job bookmarks enabled

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Glue streaming and Managed Flink process streams continuously with low latency.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A Redshift COPY command from S3 every night: Nightly COPY is batch.
• An Athena query run manually every hour: Manual hourly queries are slow.
• A daily Glue batch job with job bookmarks…: Daily batches are slow.

Key takeaway: Managed stream processing → Glue streaming or Managed Flink.
services: Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink

stem: A company needs to move 200 TB of historical files from on-premises NAS to S3 over a 10 Gbps link with scheduling and verification. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon Kinesis
AWS DataSync
AWS DMS only
AWS AppFlow

explanation:
Why this is correct:
DataSync transfers file data online with scheduling, encryption, and integrity checks.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon Kinesis: Kinesis is for streaming.
• AWS DMS only: DMS migrates databases.
• AWS AppFlow: AppFlow targets SaaS sources.

Key takeaway: Online file transfers at scale → DataSync.

stem: A Glue job needs to handle semi-structured JSON where the same field is sometimes a string and sometimes a number. Which Glue capability helps?

choices.text: DynamicFrames with resolveChoice
S3 lifecycle rules on the input files
Strict Spark DataFrame schemas only
Glue crawlers with default settings

explanation:
Why this is correct:
DynamicFrames represent ambiguous types as choices, and resolveChoice resolves them.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 lifecycle rules on the input files: Lifecycle rules manage storage.
• Strict Spark DataFrame schemas only: Strict schemas fail on inconsistent types.
• Glue crawlers with default settings: Crawlers infer schemas but do not fix records.

Key takeaway: Handle inconsistent types with DynamicFrames.

stem: A pipeline must run a Glue job every day at 02:00 UTC with minimal setup. Which TWO options fit? (Select TWO)

choices.text: A scheduled Glue trigger
An S3 lifecycle transition at 02:00
A manual start by the on-call engineer
A CloudFront cache expiration setting
An EventBridge Scheduler schedule

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Glue scheduled triggers and EventBridge Scheduler both run jobs on schedules.

Why the other options are wrong:
• An S3 lifecycle transition at 02:00: Lifecycle rules do not run jobs.
• A manual start by the on-call engineer: Manual starts are unreliable.
• A CloudFront cache expiration setting: CloudFront settings are unrelated.

Key takeaway: Schedule jobs with Glue triggers or EventBridge Scheduler.

stem: A query repeatedly computes the same expensive aggregation on Redshift data that changes a few times per day. Which feature improves performance?

choices.text: A larger node type for all queries only
A new table created manually by an analyst for each query
Exporting data to CSV before each query
A materialized view with scheduled or auto refresh

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Materialized views store precomputed results and refresh when data changes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A larger node type for all queries only: Larger nodes are costly.
• A new table created manually by an analyst…: Manual tables are error-prone.
• Exporting data to CSV before each query: CSV exports slow queries.

Key takeaway: Precompute repeated aggregations with materialized views.

stem: A company must ingest change events from a DynamoDB table into an analytics pipeline in near real time. Which source fits?

choices.text: AWS Config configuration items for the table
DynamoDB Streams or Kinesis Data Streams for DynamoDB
A daily full table scan exported to CSV files in S3
CloudTrail management events for the table

explanation:
Why this is correct:
DynamoDB change streams capture item-level changes for downstream processing.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Config configuration items for the table: Config records configuration, not items.
• A daily full table scan exported to CSV…: Daily scans are slow and costly.
• CloudTrail management events for the table: CloudTrail records API calls, not data changes.

Key takeaway: Capture DynamoDB changes with streams.

stem: Which TWO file design choices improve Athena query performance and cost? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Random file names without any partitions
One huge CSV file for all history
Columnar formats such as Parquet with compression
Many tiny uncompressed JSON files
Partitioning by commonly filtered columns

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Columnar compressed formats and partitioning reduce data scanned.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Random file names without any partitions: No partitions forces full scans.
• One huge CSV file for all history: A huge CSV forces full scans.
• Many tiny uncompressed JSON files: Tiny files add overhead.

Key takeaway: Use Parquet and partitions for Athena.

stem: A data engineer writes a Python function that reads configuration from a shared location and must be unit tested without calling AWS. Which practice helps?

choices.text: Hard-code the production credentials in the test file
Call real AWS services in every unit test run
Skip tests because the code interacts with AWS
Inject clients as parameters and use mocks or stubs in tests

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Dependency injection with mocks lets code be tested without real AWS calls.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Hard-code the production credentials in the…: Hard-coded credentials are insecure.
• Call real AWS services in every unit test run: Real calls make tests slow and flaky.
• Skip tests because the code interacts with AWS: Skipping tests allows defects.

Key takeaway: Make AWS code testable with injection and mocks.

stem: A data pipeline must publish a notification when a job fails so engineers can respond. Which approach fits?

choices.text: A dashboard showing yesterday's job counts
An S3 bucket where logs are stored for review
EventBridge rule on job state changes targeting SNS
Engineers checking the Glue console every few hours for failures

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Job state change events routed to SNS notify engineers immediately.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A dashboard showing yesterday's job counts: Dashboards do not alert.
• An S3 bucket where logs are stored for review: Stored logs do not notify.
• Engineers checking the Glue console every…: Manual checks are slow.

Key takeaway: Alert on pipeline failures via EventBridge and SNS.

stem: A Glue job loads data into Redshift. Which approach loads large volumes most efficiently?

choices.text: Stage data in S3 and use the COPY command
Insert rows one at a time with INSERT
Use SELECT INTO from a CSV string
Use UPDATE statements for new rows

explanation:
Why this is correct:
COPY loads data in parallel from S3 and is the efficient bulk load method.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Insert rows one at a time with INSERT: Row-by-row inserts are slow.
• Use SELECT INTO from a CSV string: SELECT INTO from strings is not a bulk load.
• Use UPDATE statements for new rows: UPDATE modifies existing rows.

Key takeaway: Bulk load Redshift with COPY from S3.

stem: A company receives unpredictable bursts of streaming data and wants no shard capacity planning. Which Kinesis option fits?

choices.text: A single shard with enhanced fan-out
Kinesis Data Streams on-demand mode
SQS FIFO queues with high throughput
Provisioned mode with a fixed shard count

explanation:
Why this is correct:
On-demand mode scales capacity automatically with traffic.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A single shard with enhanced fan-out: One shard limits throughput.
• SQS FIFO queues with high throughput: SQS is a different service without stream semantics.
• Provisioned mode with a fixed shard count: Fixed shards need planning.

Key takeaway: Unpredictable streams → on-demand mode.

stem: Analysts need to run complex SQL joins and aggregations over terabytes of structured data with consistent, fast performance for dashboards. Which data store fits?

choices.text: Amazon DynamoDB tables with global secondary indexes
Amazon Redshift
Amazon S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval archives
Amazon ElastiCache for Redis with sorted sets

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Redshift is a data warehouse optimized for complex analytical SQL at scale.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon DynamoDB tables with global secondary…: DynamoDB is not built for complex joins.
• Amazon S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval archives: Glacier is archival storage.
• Amazon ElastiCache for Redis with sorted sets: ElastiCache is an in-memory cache.

Key takeaway: Analytical SQL at scale → Redshift.

stem: An application needs single-digit millisecond key-value lookups at any scale for user profiles. Which store fits?

choices.text: Amazon DynamoDB
Amazon Redshift clusters with sort keys
Amazon EMR with HDFS storage volumes
Amazon Athena queries over S3 data

explanation:
Why this is correct:
DynamoDB provides consistent low-latency key-value access at scale.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon Redshift clusters with sort keys: Redshift targets analytics.
• Amazon EMR with HDFS storage volumes: EMR HDFS is for batch processing.
• Amazon Athena queries over S3 data: Athena is interactive analytics, not millisecond lookups.

Key takeaway: Low-latency key-value access → DynamoDB.

stem: A company wants a data lake that stores raw and curated data cheaply at any scale and is queryable by several engines. Which foundation fits?

choices.text: EC2 instance store volumes on a fleet
Amazon RDS for MySQL with large storage
Amazon S3 with open formats such as Parquet
Amazon EBS volumes attached to one instance

explanation:
Why this is correct:
S3 with open formats is the standard, low-cost foundation for data lakes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• EC2 instance store volumes on a fleet: Instance store is ephemeral.
• Amazon RDS for MySQL with large storage: RDS is a transactional database.
• Amazon EBS volumes attached to one instance: EBS volumes attach to single instances.

Key takeaway: Data lake foundation → S3 with open formats.

stem: Analysts want to query data in S3 from Redshift and join it with local Redshift tables without loading it. Which feature fits?

choices.text: Redshift COPY into staging tables
Redshift UNLOAD to S3 in Parquet
Redshift resize to more nodes only
Redshift Spectrum external tables

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Spectrum queries external data in S3 and can join it with local tables.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Redshift COPY into staging tables: COPY loads data.
• Redshift UNLOAD to S3 in Parquet: UNLOAD exports data.
• Redshift resize to more nodes only: Resizing does not query S3.

Key takeaway: Query S3 from Redshift with Spectrum.

stem: A data lake table must support row-level updates, deletes, and time travel on S3 while remaining queryable by Athena and Spark. Which table format fits?

choices.text: Plain CSV files in folders
Apache Iceberg tables
Unpartitioned JSON files
Excel workbooks in S3

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Iceberg provides ACID transactions, row-level changes, and time travel on data lakes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Plain CSV files in folders: CSV has no transactional updates.
• Unpartitioned JSON files: JSON files lack table semantics.
• Excel workbooks in S3: Excel files are not data lake tables.

Key takeaway: Transactional data lake tables → Iceberg.

stem: A team wants a fully managed store for Apache Iceberg tables in S3 with automatic compaction and optimized performance. Which option fits?

choices.text: Amazon Keyspaces tables
Amazon EBS gp3 volumes
Amazon S3 Tables
Amazon FSx for Windows

explanation:
Why this is correct:
S3 Tables provides managed Iceberg tables with automatic maintenance such as compaction.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon Keyspaces tables: Keyspaces is Cassandra-compatible.
• Amazon EBS gp3 volumes: EBS is block storage.
• Amazon FSx for Windows: FSx for Windows is a file system.

Key takeaway: Managed Iceberg tables → S3 Tables.

stem: A workload needs to search and analyze application logs with full-text queries and near-real-time dashboards. Which store fits?

choices.text: Amazon OpenSearch Service
Amazon RDS for Oracle
Amazon Neptune graphs
Amazon QLDB ledgers

explanation:
Why this is correct:
OpenSearch supports full-text search and log analytics dashboards.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon RDS for Oracle: RDS is transactional.
• Amazon Neptune graphs: Neptune is a graph database.
• Amazon QLDB ledgers: QLDB is a ledger database.

Key takeaway: Log search and analytics → OpenSearch.

stem: Which TWO factors should most influence the choice between Redshift provisioned clusters and Redshift Serverless? (Select TWO)

choices.text: The color of the query editor in the console
The number of analysts' laptops in the office
Whether data files use uppercase column names
Predictability and steadiness of query workloads
Need for fine-grained control over node types

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Steady workloads and node control favor provisioned clusters; variable workloads favor Serverless.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The color of the query editor in the console: UI colors are irrelevant.
• The number of analysts' laptops in the office: Laptop counts are irrelevant.
• Whether data files use uppercase column names: Column name case is irrelevant.

Key takeaway: Choose Redshift mode by workload pattern and control needs.

stem: New datasets land in S3 with unknown schemas, and analysts need them queryable in Athena. Which feature discovers schemas and registers tables?

choices.text: Amazon SNS topics
AWS Config rules
AWS Glue crawlers
Amazon SQS queues

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Crawlers infer schemas and create or update Data Catalog tables.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon SNS topics: SNS publishes messages.
• AWS Config rules: Config evaluates configurations.
• Amazon SQS queues: SQS queues messages.

Key takeaway: Discover schemas with Glue crawlers.

stem: New daily partitions are added to a table in S3, but Athena queries do not see them. Which TWO fixes work? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Convert the table's data files to CSV format immediately
Run MSCK REPAIR TABLE or ALTER TABLE ADD PARTITION
Delete the table and all underlying data
Increase the Athena query timeout setting
Use partition projection for predictable partitions

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Adding partitions to the catalog or using partition projection makes new partitions queryable.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Convert the table's data files to CSV format…: Format changes do not register partitions.
• Delete the table and all underlying data: Deleting data is destructive.
• Increase the Athena query timeout setting: Timeouts do not add partitions.

Key takeaway: Register partitions or use partition projection.

stem: A company wants a central business data catalog where analysts can discover, request access to, and subscribe to datasets. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Elastic Beanstalk environments
Amazon Lightsail databases only
Amazon CloudFront distributions
Amazon DataZone (SageMaker Catalog)

explanation:
Why this is correct:
DataZone and SageMaker Catalog provide business data catalogs with publish, discovery, and subscription workflows.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Elastic Beanstalk environments: Beanstalk deploys apps.
• Amazon Lightsail databases only: Lightsail hosts simple apps.
• Amazon CloudFront distributions: CloudFront is a CDN.

Key takeaway: Business data discovery and sharing → DataZone or SageMaker Catalog.

stem: A crawler creates many small tables instead of one partitioned table because folder structures differ slightly. Which fix helps?

choices.text: Standardize the folder layout and configure crawler grouping or table-level settings
Delete the Data Catalog entries and query the files by name without defining any tables at all
Convert every file to a different format before each crawler run
Run the crawler more often so the tables merge together over time

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Consistent layouts and crawler grouping settings create a single partitioned table.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Delete the Data Catalog entries and query…: Removing the catalog prevents querying.
• Convert every file to a different format…: Format changes do not fix layout inconsistency.
• Run the crawler more often so the tables…: Running more often does not merge tables.

Key takeaway: Consistent layouts produce clean catalog tables.

stem: Which service stores table metadata used by Athena, EMR, and Redshift Spectrum in a shared, central catalog?

choices.text: AWS Glue Data Catalog
AWS Systems Manager
Amazon Route 53
AWS Secrets Manager

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The Glue Data Catalog is a central metastore shared by many analytics services.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Systems Manager: Systems Manager manages operations.
• Amazon Route 53: Route 53 is DNS.
• AWS Secrets Manager: Secrets Manager stores secrets.

Key takeaway: Shared metastore → Glue Data Catalog.

stem: Raw data in S3 is used heavily for 30 days, then rarely, and must be kept for seven years. Which approach minimizes cost?

choices.text: Keep all data in S3 Standard for seven years
Move everything to Glacier Deep Archive on the first day after upload
Delete data after 30 days and rebuild if needed
Lifecycle rules transitioning to cheaper classes and archives over time

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Lifecycle transitions match storage classes to access patterns.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Keep all data in S3 Standard for seven years: Standard is costly for cold data.
• Move everything to Glacier Deep Archive on…: Deep Archive is slow for active data.
• Delete data after 30 days and rebuild if needed: Deleting violates retention.

Key takeaway: Tier data with lifecycle rules.

stem: A DynamoDB table stores session events that are useless after 90 days. Which feature removes them automatically at no extra cost?

choices.text: DAX caching
Global tables
Time to live (TTL)
PITR backups

explanation:
Why this is correct:
TTL deletes expired items automatically without consuming write capacity.

Why the other options are wrong:
• DAX caching: DAX caches reads.
• Global tables: Global tables replicate data.
• PITR backups: PITR supports recovery.

Key takeaway: Expire DynamoDB items with TTL.

stem: Old Redshift data is rarely queried but must remain available for occasional analysis at low cost. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Delete the old data and restore it from backups manually when needed
UNLOAD old data to S3 in Parquet and query it with Spectrum
Copy old data into DynamoDB for cheaper storage
Keep all history in hot Redshift tables forever

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Offloading cold data to S3 and querying with Spectrum reduces warehouse storage cost.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Delete the old data and restore it from…: Deleting loses accessibility.
• Copy old data into DynamoDB for cheaper storage: DynamoDB is not for analytical history.
• Keep all history in hot Redshift tables forever: Hot storage for cold data is costly.

Key takeaway: Offload cold warehouse data to S3.

stem: A company must prevent deletion or modification of compliance data in S3 for five years. Which feature fits?

choices.text: S3 Versioning without MFA Delete
S3 Object Lock in compliance mode
S3 Intelligent-Tiering archive tiers
S3 Requester Pays configuration

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Compliance mode prevents any user from deleting or overwriting objects during retention.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 Versioning without MFA Delete: Versions can still be deleted.
• S3 Intelligent-Tiering archive tiers: Tiering changes cost, not immutability.
• S3 Requester Pays configuration: Requester Pays affects billing.

Key takeaway: Immutable retention → Object Lock compliance mode.

stem: Which TWO actions reduce storage cost for a versioned S3 data lake bucket? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Replicate every object to three other Regions
Disable compression for all stored data files
Enable Transfer Acceleration for all uploads
Abort incomplete multipart uploads with a lifecycle rule
Expire noncurrent object versions after a set period

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Expiring noncurrent versions and cleaning incomplete uploads remove hidden storage waste.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Replicate every object to three other Regions: Replication multiplies storage.
• Disable compression for all stored data files: Compression reduces storage.
• Enable Transfer Acceleration for all uploads: Transfer Acceleration adds cost.

Key takeaway: Clean up hidden S3 storage waste.

stem: A source adds new columns over time. The data lake must accept them without breaking existing queries. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Store each schema version in a separate unrelated bucket
Rewrite all historical files whenever a column is added
Use formats and tables that support schema evolution, such as Parquet with Iceberg
Reject every incoming file that contains a column the pipeline has not seen before

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Schema evolution support lets new columns be added without breaking readers.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Store each schema version in a separate…: Separate buckets fragment data.
• Rewrite all historical files whenever a…: Rewriting history is costly.
• Reject every incoming file that contains a…: Rejecting files loses data.

Key takeaway: Plan for schema evolution.

stem: Streaming producers and consumers must agree on record schemas, and incompatible changes must be blocked. Which feature fits?

choices.text: AWS Glue Schema Registry with compatibility modes
A wiki page that lists the current schema fields
CloudWatch alarms on consumer error counts only
A shared spreadsheet updated by each producer team

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Schema Registry validates schemas and enforces compatibility rules.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A wiki page that lists the current schema fields: Documentation does not enforce.
• CloudWatch alarms on consumer error counts only: Alarms detect after failure.
• A shared spreadsheet updated by each…: Spreadsheets do not enforce.

Key takeaway: Enforce streaming schemas with Schema Registry.

stem: A DynamoDB access pattern requires querying orders by status and date. The table key is customer_id. What should be added?

choices.text: A second table storing the same items by hand
A local secondary index that uses status as the partition key and date as the sort key
A global secondary index with status as partition key and date as sort key
A Scan with filter expressions for every request

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A GSI supports a new access pattern with different keys.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A second table storing the same items by hand: Manual duplication is error-prone.
• A local secondary index that uses status as…: LSIs must share the table's partition key.
• A Scan with filter expressions for every request: Scans are expensive.

Key takeaway: New access patterns → GSIs.

stem: A dimensional model separates facts (sales) from dimensions (product, customer, date). What is this design called?

choices.text: Key-value model
Graph model
Document model
Star schema

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A star schema has a central fact table linked to dimension tables.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Key-value model: Key-value models store items by key.
• Graph model: Graph models store nodes and edges.
• Document model: Document models store nested documents.

Key takeaway: Facts plus dimensions → star schema.

stem: Customer addresses change, and analysts must see historical addresses at the time of each order. Which technique fits?

choices.text: Slowly changing dimension type 2 with effective dates
Overwrite the address in place for each change
Store only the current address in the fact table
Delete old orders when addresses change

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SCD type 2 keeps historical versions with effective date ranges.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Overwrite the address in place for each change: Overwriting loses history.
• Store only the current address in the fact table: Current address only loses history.
• Delete old orders when addresses change: Deleting orders loses data.

Key takeaway: Track history with SCD type 2.

stem: A time-series workload stores sensor readings and needs fast time-range queries and automatic data tiering. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Glue DataBrew
Amazon Timestream
Amazon DocumentDB
Amazon Neptune

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Timestream is purpose-built for time-series data with tiered storage.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Glue DataBrew: DataBrew prepares data.
• Amazon DocumentDB: DocumentDB is a document database.
• Amazon Neptune: Neptune is a graph database.

Key takeaway: Time-series data → Timestream.

stem: A Redshift cluster's storage fills up while compute is underused. Which option lets storage scale independently of compute?

choices.text: DC2 nodes with local SSD storage only
Moving data to EBS volumes attached manually
RA3 nodes with Redshift managed storage
Adding more DC2 nodes for disk space

explanation:
Why this is correct:
RA3 nodes separate compute from managed storage, which scales independently.

Why the other options are wrong:
• DC2 nodes with local SSD storage only: DC2 couples storage and compute.
• Moving data to EBS volumes attached manually: Redshift does not use manually attached EBS.
• Adding more DC2 nodes for disk space: More DC2 nodes add unneeded compute.

Key takeaway: Independent storage scaling → RA3 managed storage.

stem: An analytics team wants to share live Redshift data with another Redshift cluster in a different account without copying it. Which feature fits?

choices.text: Redshift resize ops
Redshift data sharing
Redshift UNLOAD jobs
Redshift snapshots

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Data sharing gives other clusters live, read access to data without copying.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Redshift resize ops: Resizing changes capacity.
• Redshift UNLOAD jobs: UNLOAD exports copies.
• Redshift snapshots: Snapshots are backups and copies.

Key takeaway: Share live warehouse data with Redshift data sharing.

stem: A company wants to replicate a DynamoDB table's data to S3 for analytics without affecting table performance. Which feature fits?

choices.text: DAX in front of the table for analytics reads
DynamoDB TTL settings on every item in the table
A full Scan running every hour against the table
DynamoDB export to S3 (point-in-time export)

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Export to S3 uses PITR data and does not consume table read capacity.

Why the other options are wrong:
• DAX in front of the table for analytics reads: DAX accelerates application reads.
• DynamoDB TTL settings on every item in the table: TTL deletes items.
• A full Scan running every hour against the table: Scans consume capacity and affect performance.

Key takeaway: Analytics copies from DynamoDB → export to S3.

stem: A zero-ETL approach is desired to make Aurora transactional data available in Redshift for analytics in near real time. Which feature fits?

choices.text: Aurora zero-ETL integration with Amazon Redshift
Manual SQL dumps imported by an analyst each morning
Nightly CSV exports copied to S3 and loaded with COPY
A Lambda function that polls Aurora every minute for rows

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Zero-ETL integrations replicate data from Aurora to Redshift without building pipelines.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Manual SQL dumps imported by an analyst each…: Manual dumps are slow.
• Nightly CSV exports copied to S3 and loaded…: Nightly exports add delay.
• A Lambda function that polls Aurora every…: Polling functions are fragile.

Key takeaway: Near-real-time Aurora to Redshift → zero-ETL integration.

stem: A workload needs a relational database for an application's transactions and must support many concurrent small reads and writes. Which store fits?

choices.text: Amazon Athena with partitions
Amazon S3 with Parquet files
Amazon Redshift with sort keys
Amazon Aurora or Amazon RDS

explanation:
Why this is correct:
OLTP workloads with frequent small transactions suit relational databases such as Aurora or RDS.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon Athena with partitions: Athena is for analytics queries.
• Amazon S3 with Parquet files: S3 files are not transactional.
• Amazon Redshift with sort keys: Redshift is for analytics.

Key takeaway: OLTP → Aurora or RDS; OLAP → Redshift.

stem: Which TWO practices improve the design of a partitioned data lake table? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Use a different partition scheme for every daily load
Partition on a unique ID column with millions of values
Partition on columns commonly used in filters, such as date
Store all partitions in a single flat folder with no layout
Avoid partitions so small that each holds only a few KB

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Useful partitions match query filters and avoid over-partitioning into tiny files.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Use a different partition scheme for every…: Inconsistent schemes break queries.
• Partition on a unique ID column with…: High-cardinality partitions create too many tiny partitions.
• Store all partitions in a single flat folder…: Flat layouts defeat partitioning.

Key takeaway: Partition on common filters with sensible granularity.

stem: Athena query planning is slow on a table with hundreds of thousands of partitions following a predictable date pattern. Which feature helps?

choices.text: Larger result files
Partition projection
Workgroup tagging
More Glue crawlers

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Partition projection computes partitions from configuration instead of loading them from the catalog.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Larger result files: Result files are unrelated.
• Workgroup tagging: Tags do not affect planning.
• More Glue crawlers: More crawlers add more partitions to load.

Key takeaway: Speed planning for many partitions with partition projection.

stem: A data lake must remove a specific customer's records to satisfy a deletion request, efficiently. Which table format helps?

choices.text: Apache Iceberg with row-level delete support
Excel files downloaded and edited on a laptop
Plain CSV files that must be rewritten by hand
Compressed JSON archives in Glacier Deep Archive

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Iceberg supports row-level deletes without manually rewriting whole datasets.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Excel files downloaded and edited on a laptop: Laptop edits are insecure.
• Plain CSV files that must be rewritten by hand: Manual rewrites are slow and error-prone.
• Compressed JSON archives in Glacier Deep Archive: Deep Archive retrieval is slow and files lack deletes.

Key takeaway: Handle deletion requests with row-level operations.

stem: A data engineer wants to automate a recurring data preparation task in Python without managing servers, triggered daily. Which TWO components fit? (Select TWO)

choices.text: EventBridge Scheduler to trigger it daily
An always-on EC2 instance with a cron job
A manual run from a laptop every morning
A Redshift cluster running the Python code
A Lambda function or Glue Python shell job

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Serverless compute triggered by a scheduler automates the task without servers.

Why the other options are wrong:
• An always-on EC2 instance with a cron job: An always-on instance requires management and costs more.
• A manual run from a laptop every morning: Manual runs are unreliable.
• A Redshift cluster running the Python code: Redshift is not a Python job runner.

Key takeaway: Automate recurring tasks with serverless compute and schedules.

stem: Analysts repeatedly run the same Athena query each morning and download results manually. Which automation fits?

choices.text: Convert the query into a spreadsheet formula that refreshes automatically
Schedule the query with EventBridge and Step Functions, writing results to S3
Ask analysts to arrive earlier so the query finishes before meetings start
Increase the Athena workgroup's data scan limit for all users each day

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A scheduled workflow runs the query and stores results automatically.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Convert the query into a spreadsheet formula…: Spreadsheet formulas cannot run Athena queries.
• Ask analysts to arrive earlier so the query…: Earlier arrival is not automation.
• Increase the Athena workgroup's data scan…: Scan limits do not automate queries.

Key takeaway: Automate recurring queries with scheduled workflows.

stem: A team wants to call Redshift SQL from a Lambda function without managing JDBC connections or drivers. Which feature fits?

choices.text: Redshift resize
Redshift snapshots
Redshift Data API
Redshift UNLOAD

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The Data API runs SQL asynchronously over HTTPS without managing connections.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Redshift resize: Resize changes capacity.
• Redshift snapshots: Snapshots back up data.
• Redshift UNLOAD: UNLOAD exports data.

Key takeaway: Serverless SQL calls to Redshift → Data API.

stem: A monthly job must start an EMR cluster, run Spark steps, and terminate the cluster when finished to save cost. Which approach fits?

choices.text: A Lambda function running the Spark job within its 15-minute limit
A long-running EMR cluster kept up all month for the single monthly job
A manually created cluster that an engineer is expected to remember to shut down after the job
Transient EMR clusters launched by Step Functions or MWAA with auto-termination

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Transient clusters run only for the job and terminate automatically.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A Lambda function running the Spark job…: Lambda cannot run large Spark jobs.
• A long-running EMR cluster kept up all month…: Always-on clusters waste money.
• A manually created cluster that an engineer…: Manual shutdowns are forgotten.

Key takeaway: Use transient EMR clusters for periodic jobs.

stem: Business users need interactive dashboards on Redshift and Athena data with row-level security per region. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Glue crawlers
Amazon Kinesis Firehose
Amazon SNS topics
Amazon Quick Sight

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Quick Sight provides BI dashboards with row-level security.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Glue crawlers: Crawlers catalog data.
• Amazon Kinesis Firehose: Firehose delivers streams.
• Amazon SNS topics: SNS sends notifications.

Key takeaway: BI dashboards with row-level security → Quick Sight.

stem: Athena queries scan too much data and cost too much. Which TWO changes reduce cost? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Remove all WHERE clauses to simplify the queries
Store the data as many small, uncompressed JSON files
Convert data to compressed Parquet and select only needed columns
Use SELECT * on every query for completeness
Partition data and filter on partition columns in queries

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Columnar formats, column pruning, and partition filters reduce bytes scanned.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Remove all WHERE clauses to simplify the queries: Removing filters scans more data.
• Store the data as many small, uncompressed…: Uncompressed small files increase cost.
• Use SELECT * on every query for completeness: SELECT * scans all columns.

Key takeaway: Reduce Athena scans with columns and partitions.

stem: A team wants to limit how much data each Athena query can scan and separate costs per team. Which feature fits?

choices.text: Athena workgroups with data usage controls
Glue job bookmarks enabled on the source data
S3 bucket versioning on results
Redshift WLM queues for Athena

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Workgroups set per-query and per-workgroup data limits and separate usage tracking.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Glue job bookmarks enabled on the source data: Bookmarks track processed data.
• S3 bucket versioning on results: Versioning keeps object versions.
• Redshift WLM queues for Athena: Redshift WLM does not govern Athena.

Key takeaway: Control Athena usage with workgroups.

stem: Short dashboard queries in Redshift wait behind long-running ETL queries. Which feature helps prioritize them?

choices.text: Removing all indexes and sort keys so that every query runs at the same speed
Workload management with separate queues or automatic WLM priorities
Converting dashboard queries into UNLOAD statements
Running ETL during business hours to finish sooner

explanation:
Why this is correct:
WLM routes queries to queues with priorities so short queries are not blocked.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Removing all indexes and sort keys so that…: Redshift does not use traditional indexes this way, and this would not help.
• Converting dashboard queries into UNLOAD…: UNLOAD exports data.
• Running ETL during business hours to finish…: Business-hours ETL increases contention.

Key takeaway: Prioritize Redshift workloads with WLM.

stem: Analysts need to explore data with SQL in notebooks that work across Redshift, Athena, and EMR in one environment. Which option fits?

choices.text: Amazon WorkDocs folders
AWS CloudShell sessions
AWS Artifact reports
Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SageMaker Unified Studio provides a single environment for data and analytics work across services.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon WorkDocs folders: WorkDocs is document storage.
• AWS CloudShell sessions: CloudShell is a command-line shell.
• AWS Artifact reports: Artifact provides compliance reports.

Key takeaway: Unified data and analytics workspace → SageMaker Unified Studio.

stem: A Redshift query joins a large fact table with a small dimension table and redistributes data each time. Which change helps?

choices.text: Use DISTSTYLE ALL for the small dimension table
Use DISTSTYLE ALL for the large fact table
Split the fact table into many small tables
Remove the sort keys from both tables

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Copying a small dimension table to every node avoids redistribution during joins.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Use DISTSTYLE ALL for the large fact table: ALL on a large table wastes storage.
• Split the fact table into many small tables: Splitting tables complicates queries.
• Remove the sort keys from both tables: Removing sort keys hurts performance.

Key takeaway: Replicate small dimensions with DISTSTYLE ALL.

stem: A Glue job fails intermittently, and engineers need its logs and metrics to diagnose the problem. Where should they look?

choices.text: The Route 53 query logs for the account
CloudWatch Logs and Glue job run metrics in CloudWatch
The AWS Billing console charges for the current month
The IAM credential report for all users

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Glue sends logs and metrics to CloudWatch for troubleshooting.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The Route 53 query logs for the account: DNS logs are unrelated.
• The AWS Billing console charges for the…: Billing does not show job errors.
• The IAM credential report for all users: Credential reports are unrelated.

Key takeaway: Troubleshoot Glue with CloudWatch logs and metrics.

stem: A Spark job on Glue fails with out-of-memory errors on the driver when collecting results. Which change helps?

choices.text: Convert the input to uncompressed JSON so it is easier to parse
Increase the number of files in the input to spread memory usage
Avoid collecting large datasets to the driver; write results out in parallel instead
Reduce the number of workers so that each remaining worker receives more memory from the shared pool

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Collecting large data to the driver exhausts memory; distributed writes avoid it.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Convert the input to uncompressed JSON so it…: Uncompressed JSON increases data size.
• Increase the number of files in the input to…: More files do not fix driver collection.
• Reduce the number of workers so that each…: Fewer workers do not help the driver.

Key takeaway: Keep large data distributed, not on the driver.

stem: A team wants alerts when a daily pipeline does not finish by 06:00. Which approach fits?

choices.text: A dashboard that the team reviews whenever someone remembers to check it during the morning
An S3 lifecycle rule that deletes incomplete output after one day
A CloudWatch alarm on a completion metric with missing data treated as breaching
A Glue crawler scheduled for 06:00 to catalog any output present

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Alarms on completion metrics, including missing data, detect late or failed runs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A dashboard that the team reviews whenever…: Dashboards need someone to look.
• An S3 lifecycle rule that deletes incomplete…: Lifecycle rules do not alert.
• A Glue crawler scheduled for 06:00 to…: Crawlers do not alert.

Key takeaway: Alert on missing completion signals.

stem: An engineer needs to know who changed a Glue job's script location last week. Which service provides this?

choices.text: Amazon Quick Sight
AWS CloudTrail
Amazon Athena
AWS Glue DataBrew

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudTrail records API calls such as UpdateJob with the caller identity.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon Quick Sight: Quick Sight builds dashboards.
• Amazon Athena: Athena queries data.
• AWS Glue DataBrew: DataBrew prepares data.

Key takeaway: Audit configuration changes with CloudTrail.

stem: Which TWO metrics are most useful for monitoring a Kinesis Data Streams consumer's health? (Select TWO)

choices.text: ReadProvisionedThroughputExceeded
S3 bucket size in bytes
Route 53 health check status
EC2 instance CPU credit balance
GetRecords.IteratorAgeMilliseconds

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Iterator age shows consumer lag, and read throttling shows capacity issues.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 bucket size in bytes: Bucket size is unrelated.
• Route 53 health check status: Health checks are unrelated.
• EC2 instance CPU credit balance: CPU credits are unrelated.

Key takeaway: Monitor stream consumer lag and throttling.

stem: A Step Functions pipeline failed at the third step. Where can the engineer see the input, output, and error of each step?

choices.text: The S3 server access logs for the pipeline's output bucket only
The AWS Health Dashboard for the account's Region
The EC2 instance system logs for unrelated servers
The execution history and event details in the Step Functions console

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Execution history shows inputs, outputs, and errors for each state.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The S3 server access logs for the pipeline's…: Access logs do not show step errors.
• The AWS Health Dashboard for the account's…: Health events cover AWS services.
• The EC2 instance system logs for unrelated…: Unrelated system logs do not help.

Key takeaway: Debug workflows with execution history.

stem: A pipeline must stop and alert if incoming data has more than 5% nulls in a required column. Which feature fits?

choices.text: An S3 lifecycle rule that deletes files with nulls
A crawler that renames columns with many nulls
A dashboard that shows null counts after data is loaded
AWS Glue Data Quality rules evaluated in the pipeline

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Data quality rules check thresholds and can fail or flag pipeline runs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• An S3 lifecycle rule that deletes files with…: Lifecycle rules do not inspect content.
• A crawler that renames columns with many nulls: Crawlers do not validate data.
• A dashboard that shows null counts after…: Post-load dashboards are too late.

Key takeaway: Gate pipelines with data quality rules.

stem: A team wants data quality rules recommended automatically from existing data statistics. Which feature fits?

choices.text: AWS Config managed rules
Glue Data Quality rule recommendations
IAM Access Analyzer checks
CloudWatch anomaly detection alarms

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Glue Data Quality can analyze data and recommend rules.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Config managed rules: Config checks resource configuration.
• IAM Access Analyzer checks: Access Analyzer checks permissions.
• CloudWatch anomaly detection alarms: Anomaly detection is for metrics.

Key takeaway: Start with recommended data quality rules.

stem: Duplicate records appear in a target table after pipeline retries. Which design prevents this?

choices.text: Disable retries so that any failed loads are simply skipped entirely by the pipeline
Increase the batch size so that retries happen less often
Make loads idempotent, for example with MERGE or upserts on a unique key
Append all records and ask analysts to remove duplicates later

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Idempotent loads keyed on unique identifiers prevent duplicates from retries.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Disable retries so that any failed loads are…: Skipping loads loses data.
• Increase the batch size so that retries…: Batch size does not prevent duplicates.
• Append all records and ask analysts to…: Manual cleanup is error-prone.

Key takeaway: Design idempotent loads.

stem: Which TWO checks validate that a load into the warehouse is complete and correct? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Compare checksums or sums of key columns
Check the size of the pipeline's log group
Check that the load job's name is unique
Check the console's color theme settings
Compare source and target row counts

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Row counts and aggregate checks confirm completeness and accuracy.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Check the size of the pipeline's log group: Log size does not validate data.
• Check that the load job's name is unique: Job names do not validate data.
• Check the console's color theme settings: Themes are irrelevant.

Key takeaway: Reconcile loads with counts and checksums.

stem: A team wants to profile a dataset to see value distributions, missing values, and outliers before building a pipeline. Which tool fits?

choices.text: Amazon Route 53 health checks
AWS Glue DataBrew profile jobs
AWS CodeDeploy deployment groups
Amazon SES email templates

explanation:
Why this is correct:
DataBrew profiling summarizes statistics, missing values, and distributions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon Route 53 health checks: Health checks monitor endpoints.
• AWS CodeDeploy deployment groups: CodeDeploy deploys applications.
• Amazon SES email templates: SES sends emails.

Key takeaway: Profile data with DataBrew.

stem: Bad records in a streaming pipeline must not stop processing, but must be kept for investigation. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Stop the entire stream and page the on-call engineer whenever a single bad record is detected
Retry invalid records forever until they eventually succeed
Silently drop invalid records without keeping any copy of them
Route invalid records to a dead-letter destination such as an S3 prefix or queue

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Dead-letter handling isolates bad records while processing continues.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Stop the entire stream and page the on-call…: Stopping the stream causes outages.
• Retry invalid records forever until they…: Infinite retries block processing.
• Silently drop invalid records without…: Dropping records loses evidence.

Key takeaway: Isolate bad records in dead-letter destinations.

stem: A data engineer needs to run a quick SQL check on the latest partition of a data lake table each hour. Which option requires the least infrastructure?

choices.text: A provisioned Redshift cluster only
An EC2 instance with a database
An Athena query triggered on a schedule
A permanently running EMR cluster

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Athena is serverless and charges per query, suited to light scheduled checks.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A provisioned Redshift cluster only: Provisioned Redshift is costly for small checks.
• An EC2 instance with a database: An EC2 database requires management.
• A permanently running EMR cluster: Always-on EMR is costly.

Key takeaway: Light scheduled SQL on S3 → Athena.

stem: Analysts want to query operational data in Aurora PostgreSQL from Redshift without copying it. Which feature fits?

choices.text: Redshift federated queries
Redshift UNLOAD
Redshift snapshots
Redshift COPY commands

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Federated queries read live data from RDS and Aurora PostgreSQL or MySQL.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Redshift UNLOAD: UNLOAD exports data.
• Redshift snapshots: Snapshots back up clusters.
• Redshift COPY commands: COPY loads data from files.

Key takeaway: Query operational databases from Redshift with federation.

stem: A Lambda function processing S3 events sometimes times out on large files. Which change helps?

choices.text: Increase timeout and memory, or move large-file processing to Glue or Fargate
Disable S3 event notifications for large files only
Decrease the function's timeout so that failures on large files happen faster
Remove error handling so the function finishes sooner

explanation:
Why this is correct:
More resources or a better-suited compute service handles large files.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Disable S3 event notifications for large…: Disabling events skips data.
• Decrease the function's timeout so that…: Shorter timeouts cause more failures.
• Remove error handling so the function…: Removing error handling hides problems.

Key takeaway: Match compute to file size.

stem: A pipeline should detect sudden drops in daily record counts, which may indicate upstream failures. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Look at the record counts only during monthly business reviews
Track record counts as metrics and alarm on anomalies or thresholds
Assume counts are correct as long as the pipeline job succeeds
Delete days with low counts from the table without investigation

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Monitoring volume metrics catches silent upstream failures.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Look at the record counts only during…: Monthly reviews are too late.
• Assume counts are correct as long as the…: Successful jobs can still load incomplete data.
• Delete days with low counts from the table…: Deleting data hides problems.

Key takeaway: Monitor data volume, not just job status.

stem: A company wants to automate EMR cluster sizing so it adds capacity during heavy Spark stages and removes it afterward. Which feature fits?

choices.text: EMR security configurations
EMR bootstrap actions
EMR step concurrency only
EMR managed scaling

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Managed scaling adjusts cluster capacity based on workload.

Why the other options are wrong:
• EMR security configurations: Security configurations set encryption and authentication.
• EMR bootstrap actions: Bootstrap actions run setup scripts.
• EMR step concurrency only: Step concurrency runs steps in parallel without resizing.

Key takeaway: Resize EMR automatically with managed scaling.

stem: A dashboard query in Quick Sight is slow because it queries Athena directly for each view. Which feature improves performance?

choices.text: Use a larger number of dashboard sheets
Increase the Athena query timeout setting
Import data into SPICE with scheduled refreshes
Remove filters from the dashboard visuals

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SPICE is an in-memory engine that serves dashboards quickly from imported data.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Use a larger number of dashboard sheets: More sheets do not speed queries.
• Increase the Athena query timeout setting: Timeouts do not speed queries.
• Remove filters from the dashboard visuals: Removing filters increases data.

Key takeaway: Speed dashboards with SPICE.

stem: Which TWO practices improve the maintainability of data pipelines? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Undocumented dependencies between jobs
Structured logging with correlation IDs per run
Manual edits to production scripts in the console
Hard-coded credentials in job scripts
Versioned pipeline code and configuration in source control

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Structured logs aid troubleshooting, and version control enables safe changes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Undocumented dependencies between jobs: Undocumented dependencies cause failures.
• Manual edits to production scripts in the…: Console edits cause drift.
• Hard-coded credentials in job scripts: Hard-coded credentials are insecure.

Key takeaway: Log well and version pipeline code.

stem: A team wants anomaly detection on data quality metrics over time without defining fixed thresholds for every column. Which feature fits?

choices.text: S3 Storage Lens dashboards
Route 53 traffic flow policies
VPC Flow Logs analysis
Glue Data Quality anomaly detection

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Glue Data Quality can learn patterns and detect anomalies in data statistics.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 Storage Lens dashboards: Storage Lens reports storage usage.
• Route 53 traffic flow policies: Traffic flow is DNS routing.
• VPC Flow Logs analysis: Flow Logs capture network traffic.

Key takeaway: Detect data anomalies without fixed thresholds.

stem: An analyst needs to explore a sample of large JSON files quickly with SQL and no infrastructure. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon EC2 with MySQL
Amazon EMR on EC2
Amazon Athena
Amazon Redshift RA3

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Athena runs serverless SQL directly on data in S3.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon EC2 with MySQL: A self-managed database requires setup.
• Amazon EMR on EC2: EMR requires clusters.
• Amazon Redshift RA3: Redshift requires loading or external tables and provisioning.

Key takeaway: Ad hoc SQL on S3 → Athena.

stem: A Glue job's run time doubled after data volume grew. Which TWO actions can help? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Increase workers or use Glue auto scaling
Reduce the number of workers to one
Convert the input to many tiny files
Remove job bookmarks to reprocess all data
Optimize partitioning and file sizes of inputs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
More capacity and better data layout improve job performance.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Reduce the number of workers to one: Fewer workers slow jobs.
• Convert the input to many tiny files: Tiny files add overhead.
• Remove job bookmarks to reprocess all data: Reprocessing all data increases run time.

Key takeaway: Scale workers and fix data layout.

stem: A company wants reusable, parameterized SQL transformations orchestrated as part of a data pipeline with version control. Which practice fits?

choices.text: Email SQL scripts to analysts who run them by hand
Paste the SQL into the query console each time and edit the values manually for each run
Store SQL in a repository and run it through an orchestrator with parameters
Keep SQL only in the query history of the editor

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Versioned, parameterized SQL run by an orchestrator is repeatable and reviewable.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Email SQL scripts to analysts who run them…: Emailing scripts is unmanaged.
• Paste the SQL into the query console each…: Manual edits are error-prone.
• Keep SQL only in the query history of the editor: Query history is not version control.

Key takeaway: Version and orchestrate SQL transformations.

stem: Which approach best documents where a dataset came from and how it was transformed?

choices.text: The file name of the output dataset only
The date the dataset was last modified
A comment written in one engineer's local notebook file
Data lineage captured in the catalog or governance tool

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Lineage records sources and transformations for traceability.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The file name of the output dataset only: File names do not describe transformations.
• The date the dataset was last modified: Modification dates lack context.
• A comment written in one engineer's local…: Local comments are not shared.

Key takeaway: Track data lineage centrally.

stem: A Glue job needs to read from one S3 bucket and write to another. How should it authenticate?

choices.text: An IAM role assigned to the Glue job with scoped S3 permissions
An IAM user's access keys hard-coded in the Glue job script
A public bucket policy so the job needs no credentials
The root user's credentials passed as job parameters

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Glue jobs assume an IAM role that provides temporary, scoped credentials.

Why the other options are wrong:
• An IAM user's access keys hard-coded in the…: Hard-coded keys leak.
• A public bucket policy so the job needs no…: Public buckets expose data.
• The root user's credentials passed as job…: Root credentials must never be used.

Key takeaway: Data jobs authenticate with IAM roles.

stem: A Glue job connects to an RDS database that requires a username and password. Where should the credentials be stored?

choices.text: In the Glue job's description field in the console
AWS Secrets Manager, referenced by the Glue connection
In plain text within the Glue job's Python script
In a CSV file stored in the job's input bucket

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Glue connections can retrieve credentials from Secrets Manager securely.

Why the other options are wrong:
• In the Glue job's description field in the…: Descriptions are visible to viewers.
• In plain text within the Glue job's Python…: Plain text in scripts leaks.
• In a CSV file stored in the job's input bucket: Files in buckets are not secret stores.

Key takeaway: Store database credentials in Secrets Manager.

stem: Analysts sign in with corporate identities and need Redshift access mapped to their groups. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Give every analyst superuser access to the cluster
Federate identity with IAM Identity Center or SAML and map groups to Redshift roles
Create one shared Redshift database user whose password is given to all of the analysts
Email each analyst a database password once a year

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Federation maps corporate identities and groups to database roles without shared credentials.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Give every analyst superuser access to the…: Superuser access violates least privilege.
• Create one shared Redshift database user…: Shared users remove accountability.
• Email each analyst a database password once…: Emailed passwords are insecure.

Key takeaway: Federate analyst access to the warehouse.

stem: A data lake must grant analysts access to specific tables and columns, managed centrally rather than in bucket policies. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Lake Formation permissions
EC2 security groups
S3 bucket ACLs per object
Route 53 private zones

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Lake Formation provides centralized table-, column-, and row-level permissions for data lakes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• EC2 security groups: Security groups control network traffic.
• S3 bucket ACLs per object: Object ACLs are coarse and hard to manage.
• Route 53 private zones: Private zones are DNS.

Key takeaway: Fine-grained data lake permissions → Lake Formation.

stem: Analysts in each region should see only rows for their own region in a shared data lake table. Which feature fits?

choices.text: Asking analysts to add a WHERE clause for their region
A separate S3 bucket copied for every region's analysts
Column masking that hides the region column from users
Lake Formation data filters with row-level security

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Row-level data filters restrict rows by condition centrally.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Asking analysts to add a WHERE clause for…: Voluntary filters are not enforcement.
• A separate S3 bucket copied for every…: Copying data creates sprawl.
• Column masking that hides the region column…: Hiding a column does not restrict rows.

Key takeaway: Enforce row-level access with Lake Formation data filters.

stem: A company wants to manage data lake permissions at scale using attributes such as department and sensitivity. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Individual grants for every user on every table
Public tables readable by everyone in the org
Lake Formation tag-based access control (LF-TBAC)
One administrator role shared by all analysts

explanation:
Why this is correct:
LF-Tags assign attributes to resources and grant access by tags, scaling permission management.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Individual grants for every user on every table: Individual grants do not scale.
• Public tables readable by everyone in the org: Public access exposes data.
• One administrator role shared by all analysts: Shared admin roles violate least privilege.

Key takeaway: Scale data permissions with LF-Tags.

stem: Which TWO controls restrict which columns analysts can query in Redshift? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Automatic table optimization
Sort key choices on columns
DISTKEY choices on the table
Dynamic data masking policies
Column-level GRANT privileges

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Column-level grants limit access, and masking policies hide sensitive values.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Automatic table optimization: Automatic optimization affects performance.
• Sort key choices on columns: Sort keys affect performance.
• DISTKEY choices on the table: Distribution keys affect performance.

Key takeaway: Restrict columns with grants and masking.

stem: Data in S3 must be encrypted with keys the company controls and whose use is logged. Which option fits?

choices.text: Client-side encoding with base64
SSE-KMS with a customer managed key
No encryption with versioning
SSE-S3 with Amazon managed keys

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Customer managed KMS keys give control and log usage in CloudTrail.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Client-side encoding with base64: Base64 is encoding, not encryption.
• No encryption with versioning: Versioning is not encryption.
• SSE-S3 with Amazon managed keys: SSE-S3 does not provide customer key control.

Key takeaway: Controlled, auditable encryption → SSE-KMS with CMKs.

stem: A high-volume S3 workload using SSE-KMS generates many KMS requests and costs. Which feature reduces KMS calls?

choices.text: S3 Bucket Keys
S3 Select queries
S3 Object Lock
S3 Access Points

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Bucket Keys reduce KMS requests by using a bucket-level key to generate data keys.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 Select queries: S3 Select filters objects.
• S3 Object Lock: Object Lock prevents deletion.
• S3 Access Points: Access Points manage access paths.

Key takeaway: Cut KMS request costs with S3 Bucket Keys.

stem: Analysts should see only the last four digits of credit card numbers in query results. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Encrypt the column and give analysts the decryption key
Store card numbers in a separate bucket with public access
Dynamic data masking or masking transforms before exposing data
Rename the column so analysts do not recognize it

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Masking reveals only permitted portions of sensitive values.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Encrypt the column and give analysts the…: Giving keys reveals full values.
• Store card numbers in a separate bucket with…: Public buckets expose data.
• Rename the column so analysts do not…: Renaming is obscurity.

Key takeaway: Mask sensitive values for analysts.

stem: Connections from clients to Redshift must be encrypted. Which setting enforces this?

choices.text: Enable concurrency scaling on the cluster
Enable automated snapshots on the cluster
Enable enhanced VPC routing on the cluster
Set require_ssl to true in the cluster parameter group

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The require_ssl parameter forces clients to connect with TLS.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Enable concurrency scaling on the cluster: Concurrency scaling adds capacity.
• Enable automated snapshots on the cluster: Snapshots are backups.
• Enable enhanced VPC routing on the cluster: Enhanced VPC routing affects COPY/UNLOAD traffic paths.

Key takeaway: Enforce TLS to Redshift with require_ssl.

stem: Auditors need a record of who accessed specific objects in a sensitive S3 bucket. Which feature fits?

choices.text: CloudTrail data events for the bucket
CloudTrail management events only
S3 Storage Lens usage dashboards
S3 Inventory reports by prefix

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudTrail data events record object-level API calls such as GetObject.
